Mr. Jordan remodeled the house taking down the two upper stories of the house. The only originals still on the Cadman Home grounds are 3 pine trees that stand in the front yard. This area the Cadman Home stands on which could have been a Way Station and Trading Post on the cut off of the Oregon Trail. The fire moves all around, the hot spot. They are similar to the Tunnel Kiln only in the Tunnel Kiln you move the ware through the fire zone, on railroad cars. Where the round down drafts are just a done, they are completely hollow, but the floor is a grid and under the floor is a connection to the smoke stack. You start your fires in the outer wall, through openings in the outer wall, heat comes in, then there is what is called a bag wall up to the crown. The fire is through this wall and the heat reflected up way, the draft being down the fire goes down through the brick from the top down, then out through the stack. The reason, as you know, heat rises, so you have to circulate it to get the heat to the bottom. Otherwise, all the heat would be up in the top and very little at the bottom. So, by that way you get a very even fire. You put your ware in all green and all cold. You start your fires and suck the heat down build up the temperature and it forms a glass substance. Brick is just hard glass. Then you cool the whole thing down and take the ware out and put new ware in, and that is called a periodic, where it 1S fired and cooled off. HAROLD BAUER: Harold Gana) Bauer. But everybody calls me Hal or Cal. STAN TALLEY: You know, I ve known you quite well for the last five years and I know it s always’ been Hal Bauer, so I didn t know whether it was Harold or Hal. Well, Harold, can you tell me, how long have you lived in this part of town. HAROLD BAUER: All my life, is, uh, 72 and a half years, aside from the time I spent in the Army, that was three and a half years, and, uh, either four or six months in California, during the Depression I couldn t find a job. I had been told that, uh, men were out on the street corners selling apples and newspapers. I thought, boy, if jobs are that plentiful, I m gonna go. So, when I got out there, I found out that these men selling apples and newspapers, that s all they had to do, they couldn t find anything else, so I was a sucker. STAN TALLEY: Can you tell me what year that was? HAROLD BAUER: About 1938. STAN: I m sure you remember in conversation with your folks, did they tell you where they came from and how they got to this part of the country? HAROLD: Yes, they came from, uh, the Bauer s came from Frank(?), Russia, and the Ames came from Walter(?),Russia, and, uh, they came by, uh, ship to America, but I don t remember exactly from what port they came in Europe, and then when they got to New York they came here to Lincoln, and that s where they settled. STAN: Can you tell me about what year that was? HAROLD: Oh, I m not sure, but I ve got records, I could look it up if you want. STAN: Could you just guess and say an approximate date? Were they married over there or over here? HAROLD: Well, my grandfather and grandmother were married in Russia and came over, and then they, quite a few of the children were born in Russia, too, like my. Father and some of the aunts were born in Russia, and, uh, my grandfather had one daughter living with him, that as far as I know had never been married. STAN: So your parents were married after they got to this country. HAROLD: Yes, they got married over here. STAN: Was it in this part of town? SSCCO, #012, page 2 HAROLD: Right in this neighborhood. Yes, sir. I don t know if they had, uh, a house wedding, or a tent wedding, a tent wedding was real popular at that time, and, uh, three to five days and nights. They d set a tent in the yard and the older women would do the cooking and when they didn t have to do any cooking or baking or anything, they d be sitting around the edges of the tent inside while the others were dancing and they d be chewing these sunflower seeds, and, uh, it was really something. I saw some of those weddings, but, uh, I don t remember who they were. STAN: I can remember when I was youngster that I attended one of those weddings and I know about what they re like, they re something. HAROLD: Yes, use a copper boiler for cooking soup. STAN: Do you remember what your father did for a living? HAROLD: Yes, he started out working for, uh, Mr. C. H. Bauer. He had a paint factory and also a grocery store and he also did coffe roasting. He was quite a promoter. My Father worked in the paint factory, mixing paint and, uh, grinding material, whatever needed, and he also did some of the glass work when it needed, you know, and later on, he got to working with the Burlington Railroad as a car checker down at the freight house, and then, he wasa good carpenter and craftsman so, after he got out of the Burlington he found a better job out at the Burlington yards. He was a car carpenter and later on became a cab carpenter, putting the glass in the cabs and sewing the canvas curtains for the old steam engines, to keep the engineer and fireman warm, well, at least it helped. STAN: You ve reached back quite a ways then. Hal, do you have any idea as to the time frame, do you have any idea about how old your parents were when they came to this country? Or your father at any rate. HAROLD: Oh, let s see, my Father might have been, uh, eight or ten years old, I don t know, I might be able to find out. And my Mother about the same, she was only two or three years less. STAN: How old would they be now, about? HAROLD: Well, my Father would be, uh, about 97 or 8 years old. My Mother I don t know, I d have to look that up, too. STAN: What I was really after was that that makes your roots in the community reach back almost a hundred years. Ze HAROLD: Oh, 4 , yes. STAN: Do you remember what the town and the area used to look like, say 60, 70 years ago? HAROLD: Well, there were quite a few houses in the neighborhood, and my Father told about when they first came here, there were just a few houses in this neighborhood, and then they had, uh, I think the Burlington had a storage track on 5th Street here, where they stored cars, and there was a ice house, uh, in this neighborhood north of here maybe a block or two. SSCCO, #012, page 3 STAN: And the address here is what? HAROLD: 429 E. STAN: 429 E Street. In otherwords, you re saying just north of here a ways there was an ice house. HAROLD: An ice house, he used to tell us about. STAN: And the 5th Street tracks, as they exist today, were in existance back then? HAROLD: As far as I know, they were. STAN: Do you remember when they put in the other trackage down here? HAROLD: — No, © don t. STAN: Do you know, was the 3rd Street track about like it is now, as you remember it, as far back as you remember? HAROLD: Well, it s, uh, as far as I know it s the same track except that they ve improved it by putting in heavier pwaunty iiny and, uh, I remember there used to be what we called the, uh, oh, i was one coach that carried passengers and it also had mail and baggage, ran from Lincoln down into Kansas or Missouri someplace. I think it left every morning and came back in the evening. Oh, we used to call it the motorcar. It was, uh, gasoline, if I m right, it was gasoline powered, and it was a pretty good sized motorcar. STAN: I ve been told earlier that the 3rd Street track didn t run all the way south to begin with, that they, it just went a little ways, and then, just for a holding track, and then finally they added to it. HAROLD: That might be, but I don t know. STAN: That would have been before your time, HAROLD: Well, it might have been in my time but I didn t know anything about it, you see. STAN: What about the 4th Street track, the Union Pacific track? HAROLD: Well, that s the one this motorcar used to run on, uh, I made a mistake when I said 3rd Street. STAN: Oh, it was the 4th Street track. HAROLD: 4th Street, Union Pacific, usedto run the motorcar. STAN: Back a ways when you were a youngster, how different is the park today than it used to be? HAROLD: F Street Park? It was much different. On the, uh, northwest corner there was a big, uh, domed, it was a cistern, City water, A B14 SSCCO, #012, page 4 HAROLD eats it was covered over with, uh, oh, Detiats and roofingpratt tA Ot whee nee: and this was a pretty big, it was deep and, uh,. pretty ood band, and right east of that there was a brick pbuilding, that had the, uh, pumps in it for pumping City water, and I think it also generated some electric. And then the, uh, the park had a grandstand in the center where we used to go up and hear the bands play on Sunday and sometimes on special holiday evening, you know, and there was also a small building there for selling pop and candy and different things, ice cream. And the park was, uh, ran from 8th Street to 6th Street and, uh, it was almost level, but on 6th Street here there was quite a hill, where you had to either slide down or roll down, you couldn t walk, and later on they put a set of concrete steps in there, right even with E Street so you could walk up the side of the hill, and, uh, the kids got there, by hand they destroyed that bandstand and also tore down the old ice cream stand, and later on the City and Parks Department put in some benches where you could sit around, you know, and have your picnic lunch or whatever, and then the Cooper Foundation got a hold of it and they made big improvements there. STAN: Then there were a few ornery kids around back in that day too? HAROLD: Oh, lots of ‘tem. Why they tore down the grandstand, I don t rightly know, something ..4 7A sof fey you know. STAN: Can you tell me, where did you first begin going to school? HAROLD: Up here at Park School. STAN: Right here at Park School. HAROLD: Yes, sir, there was a either a two or three story pilates, yellow brick, or yellow painted brick, and, uh, went to school there for a few years, and, uh, one morning we heard, no school today, ran out, school burned last night, so everybody was happy, somebody set the building afire and it burned up quite abitof it, and, uh, like yesterday and today, I remember one morning we got up and, uh, there was about a half to three quarter inch of ice on everything, on the paving, sidewalk, anyplace you wanted to go. So, I put on my skatesand I skated to school. STAN: So you skated all the way up there. HAROLD: Sure. Over grass and everything. Skated on up to ee and, uh, recess time we came out and skated some more. I don t remember now how I got home, I think it started to melt. STAN: Did you go to school in the new school then? HAROLD: Well, let s see, no, not in this new one. From Park I went to, uh, McKinley, it was called McKiniey Junior High. STAN: Where was that? HAROLD: Up on, uh, I believe from 15th to 16th on M and N. STAN: When you were a youngster going to school, in the community SSCCO, #012, page 5. STAN cont.: or in the City, per se, of Lincoln, were there a lot ' of other schools? : HAROLD: Well, there was, uh, Longfellow down on about lst and, uh, lst and J or K, and if I remember right, the one out at West A, Willard, and, uh, Park School and Everett and, uh, the, uh, McKinley Junior High, and the, uh, Emanuel Lutheran Church, they had their own school on 8th and B, what is now the American Forward building, they had their church there and they also taught their children in school there, and, uh, we, we always thought because they were in their own school that they weren t learning anything, but I ll have to give those people credit because a lot of ‘em learned, they learned the beautiful handwriting, if they didn t learn anything else, at least they learned to write good. STAN: Then actually, Lincoln, at that time, now I m talking about 55, 60 years ago, it had quite a number of schools within the area. HAROLD: Yes, there were quite a few, and then there was Capitol School, too, I forgot to mention that, and, uh. . STAN: How did it happen you didn t go to Everett Junion High? HAROLD: Well, I was supposed to, but, uh, somehow they changed it, and sent us over to McKinley. STAN: Hal, what did you do after you got out of school? Where did you work? HAROLD: About the first job I got after being a newspaper carrier for a couple of years, I got on with the Burlington, I was a messenger, down at the freight house. I carried mail to the different offices and picked it up, and, uh, back and forth from the freight house to the yard office, and, uh, while I was workin' there, later on I got to work sometime as a car sealer also a car checker, I was checking the, uh, the numbers and destination and sealing them, and, uh, I also worked for a while as a, uh, a yard, checking out the yards where you had to go out and go out to all the tracks and put down the cars numbers and what they were, like Burlington or UP, and what their destination was if they were empty or loaded, whatever, and, uh, I worked for a while at the store house and also worked on the section. STAN: How old were you then? HAROLD: Oh, about 13 or 20. STAN: How long did you work for the railroad? HAROLD: Well, in all, I d say about six years. With all the different jobs together. STAN: What did you do when you left the railroad, go in the Army? HAROLD: No, I worked for H. J. Amen in the grocery store, and that was about, uh, about nine years in all. From there I was drafted I was, had two deferements, then I was drafted and went in the Army, and I spent three and a half years there. SSCCO, #012, page 6 STAN: Where were you? Were you overseas? HAROLD: Yes, sir, saw a lot of this country and then we were sent over to, uh, to overseas, we landed in Glasgow, Scotland, and overnight we came down the southern part of England. We were there for awhile, and we had, uh, we had charge of the supply dump. Then after the invasion we supplied the different, uh, groups that came through, like with flashlights or wire or pliers, tools, anything we had, we had to keep a record of it, supply them, they were on their way to the invasion then. After the invasion a few days, we were sent over to France, and, uh, I spent about a year in Paris, France, living there, working . After we got to where we were eligible to be discharged, then I moved around a little more and finally came home. STAN: Was that after, were you in France or in Paris when the War was over, or while it was going on? HAROLD: Right after, right after the invasion, the War was still going on. STAN: Then all the time that our troops were going across France into Germany, you were in Paris. HAROLD: Yes, in Paris, and we were running a, uh, a communication system for the railroads over there in Europe. STAN: Still for the railroad. HAROLD: Yeah, we were working for the rail battalion, we had, uh, telegraph and then later on they gave us, uh, teletype to use, and we .hooked that to a lot of these small towns in Paris and different places, I mean around Paris, and we, we d set up the teletypes so you could talk to, uh, or write messages to maybe six or eight at one time. They had a big switchboard, and, uh, they made a teletype operator out of me, too, I was at first a radio repairman and, uh, they made a teletype operator out of me, and when that wasn t needed anymore then I became a messenger, rode with the mail clerk and delivered mail to the far out stations. STAN: Did you learn to play when you were in France? Either the organor... HAROLD: No, I went, I had practiced a lot over here in America before I went over in the Army, but when I was in Paris I did go to accordion school and practice once in a while. Paid for a lesson but the instructor was never there so I just practiced on my own STAN: What did you do when you got back out of the Army? HAROLD: Then I got a job working for Bill and Jack Schmall(?), they were running a business of, uh, installing gas furnaces, all kinds of jobs. STAN: Natural gas? Jimminy Christmas, there was an old fella, oh, he lived over there where Harry Brink(?)'s folks lived in a shack, and his wife had just had a baby, he backed the team up toothe front porch and went in and just took the mattress and Mom and her baby and carried it out and laid it in the wagon, went in to get another bigger baby, you know, the water wasn t in the house yet, when he come back the wagon box was floatin' down the field and the one horse had got tangled up, he was blind you know, in them days there was a lot of blind horses, and he drowned it, he took them two little kids, put ‘em in a pillowslip and crawled up the telegraph pole and hung ‘em on a, you know, hand arm and then run down the street after the wagon box to catch the boat, or it looked like a boat you know. JO: Now, who did this? GEORGE: Oh, I don t know what the old feller s name was, he wasn t an old man, hevwas a young guy, and caught the wagon box that his wife and newborn baby were in. JO: So, she was OK? GEORGE: Yeah, scared like all get out, but they made it. All of the South Bottoms they was surrounded, well, the flood in, was it '51 or 2, Johnny Johnson and his wife drownded on South 14th Street this Side of turnpike, there was somebody else out there drownded, I think that boy s name was Allen, young married fella. Water is somethin', I m gonna tell you somethin'. Water is somethin' that people don t think ‘til they see it, and you can t tell where borders are in water, you can t tell. JO: Well, George, you were confirmed here? GEORGE: Yes, Arnold, John Arnold. JO: What church were you confirmed in? GEORGE: Well, Wacker is there now on 10th and Charleston. JO: At Emmanuel Reform? You were confirmed there? What year was that, do you recall? GEORGE: Yeah, that was in 1916. JO; How long did you have to study to be confirmed? GEORGE: Well, in them days, we started in September, soon s American school started, we had four nights every week, 'til Palm Sunday, about an hour and a half every night, four nights a week, from them to Palm Sunday. JO: And then on Palm Sunday you were confirmed. Well, what kind of a celebration was it for you? GEORGE: Oh, then you was considered an adult. NBCO, #004, page 14 JO: And did your family celebrate? GEORGE: No, no, my family wasn t much for celebratin’. JO: Did your family celebrate Easter, Christmas? GEORGE: Not to what the word celebration goes, they kept it holy, that s what they did, but not celebrate, they didn t do no celebratin' at our house. : JO: Can you tell me about a Christmas at your house? GEORGE: Oh, like they were all over, you had a few little gifts, and it was somethin' ‘that was holy, considered holy, not, now a days it s altogether different. JO: You went to church? GEORGE: Oh, yes. I went to church all the time ‘til I got so I can t hear anything. JO: I mean on Christmas. GEORGE: Oh, yes, Christmas Eve, you know, they had their big program. JO: Was the food special on Christmas? GEORGE: Oh, yes, yes, your Mama always had somethin' special for, oh, there was a dozen different days of the year, and I don t know what the days all meant, ,» did you know what that meant? They had » you know. ESTHER STURTZ: Good Friday. GEORGE: And that was, oh, that had to be, and ; that hadda be, I don' + know why, put. . ESTHER STURTZ: No meat. GEORGE: And I don t think anybody cooks any more do they? ESTHER STURTZ: I do. GEORGE: You do? JO: Did your narents go to prayer meetings? GEORGE: Oh, yes, they did in the Old Country already. JO: When they came here was the Journal, the newspaper, did they start reading the newspaper here? GEORGE: No, no, we never had a newspaper 'til us kids could pay for it. Well, that wasn t their way of doing things. If we would live like our parents did, you know, spend no money only for what they d spend money for, the bare necessities, we d all be millionnaires. They never spent money and theynever threw nothin' away unless it NBCO, #004, page 15 GEORGE cont.: was wore out. There was no such a thing as style, that, there was no such a thing. When they bought somethin', they bought it and used it ‘til it was wore out. When they threw it away then nobody picked it up to make anything out of it. Why the way they throw away clothes now, you know why. But that s the way of life. Our parents wouldn t thought no more of goin' in debt to buy an automobile, why, you couldn t a got them to buy an automobile and go in debt for it like kids now a days, the hard time they have makin' a down payment. My Dad never owned a car in his life and he still have a few dollars left when he died. And he died two days before he was 84, that last six years. JO: When did you meet your wife? GEORGE: Oh, back im the: "30 s. JO: Is she from down here? GEORGE: No, Harbine, that s a town about 20 miles west of Beatrice. JO: How did you meet her? GEORGE: Oh I got around some. JO: So you had to go all the way to Harbine to see her? GEORGE: Yeah. But that wasn t very far. That old Ford I had used to take it 58 minutes from Lincoln to go to Harbine. I bought a new Ford in '36, Ford coupe. The old Model A couldn t make it that fast. JO: Well, George who is best remembered, who do you best remember in your family s history? GEORGE: Oh, I was kind of a daddy s boy. JO: So you remember daddy. GEORGE: Daddy. Yeah, I was kind of a daddy s boy. JO: Well, your father apparently was a pretty active man. Did he participate in any activities in the community? GEORGE: They were religious. It was church and prayer meeting and that was it. JO: Probably didn t have ime for anything else. GEORGE: No, that s right, and everything, you know, the way they done it, labor was not considered anything. They never bought no gas like we do to burn in the house, they burned railroad ties. They d chop ‘em up and cut ‘em up, you did that by hand, 'cause it didn t cost nothing, and that s the way it was done, that was customary. My sister just older than I, the ome: that lives at Harvard, Nebraska, Elizabeth, her and I cut many a railroad tie, when we was kids. And then, you know, my Dad had a team of horses, he brought home a lot of wood, you know, or you d buy NBCO, #004, page 16 GEORGE cont.: it you know. See in them days they never had forms to pour concrete, they hadda build 'em out of lumber, well, about the third time you use it, it s kindlin" wood, well, and it s a little kidlin' wood here and a little kindlin' wood there and if you had your own transportation, why you could keep haulin' it in about as fast as you d use it, and he d haul railroad ties for the section men and some for himself and that way the section men had fuel and he had fuel. He wouldn t stop to think how they done things, but that was customary. JO: Well, when, in other word, your parents taught you values, and when they said do something, you did it. Have you maintained any of those values? GEORGE: It s hard to explain, when you go to buy some thin' now, what you have to pay for it, you just can t explain it, ‘cause the way we were raised, until these last few years, you know, $70 for = pair of shoes or somethin’ like that, or six thousand dollars for an automobile, why, it just, well, it just don t you can t imagine that it could be possible, and you wonder once in a while what s gonna happen. I ve seen land sell, that today the taxes per acre are higher on the land than the land sold form im "3. JO:: Do you remember any of your parents' restrictions that they placed on you when you were little? GEORGE: Oh! You better be in the house around 8 30 at night, oh, boy, and the smaller ones, they never went out after supper. And even the big ones, after they was big, you d better be home at 9 00 JO: Any others? GEORGE: Well, that s the way it was. I turned down two dates where I had a date with a girl and the woman told, the mother said to the girl, now, you have her home by that time I ll have to break my neck drivin" a car to get where we re goin’ and get back so we just stayed home, never went. You couldn t drive ten miles and back in the time that she wanted her daughter back home. That happened twice to me. That s the way it was in them days. JO: When you were small, did you have any kind of a real ideal goal of what you wanted to do? GEORGE: Yeah, I wanted to farm, I farme? in to the '30 s. JO: You picked a bad time, huh? GEORGE Oh, yes. JO: So after that you didn t want to farm any more? NBCO, #004, page 17 GEORGE: The way the wind blew yesterday, a hundred and two degrees, and the wind blew like it did, if you wouldn t have irrigation, like yesterday, that d finish corn. See, that was all dry land, we didn t have this hybrid seed like they have now, it was all open pollinated, it was all together different from what it is now. And we farmed with horses then. JO: How many acres did you farm? GEORGE: Three hundred and twenty. JO: Did you have any help? GEORGE: No, only like at harvest time, sometimes at corn pickin' time, you didn t, I don t know, I never raised enough corn to have to hire help, only about two years, in the ten years I farmed. I don t know, when you look back you don t think it s possible the way things were and the way they are now. JO:. Yeah, things have really changed. The way you grew up and the way things are now, do you see an improvement, do you think it s better off or what? GEORGE: If it was just this country, I d say, it s a lot worse than it used to be. But it s that way, the world over. JO: Worse in what way? GEORGE: Well, now you need a wheelbarrow full of money to buy anything and it used to be you could carry it in the palm of your hand when you wanted to buy somethin'. You don t buy much of an automobile now for six thousand dollars and you used to buy a good car for six hundred. JO: Well, with inflation, we talk about money though, our infla- : tion, we get a lot of money but it still costs a lot of money to live. GEORGE: It ain t only the United States though, Japan and all them other countries, they have it, too, so, I don t know, I don t understand it, to me, I don t know, to me it seems impossible, but to the younger generation, why, I guess, it seems like a bed of roses. Look at my boy the kind of money he makes, they just things that s, and the wages they make now a days, why, different than when you worked for three dollars a week, sixty hours a week. END OF SIDE B JO: George, tell us all that you can remember about the beet fields. GEORGE: Well, that wasn t so bad, goin" to the beet fields, if the kids were all big enough. But then people that went who had little fellas, that was awful, I thought. In the first place, half of them farmers didn t have decent houses for themselves, let alone for the beet tender to live in, them old shanties, and they had no transportation after they were out there, and it was NBCO, #004, page 18 | GEORGE cont.: rough on the kids 'cause they left here the middle of May and got back here anywhere from the first to the middle of November and the kids that were big enough not to go to school anymore they never could get a job where they could work up to learn somethin", ‘cause they wouldn t hardly get started at a job and they went back to the beet fields. But it was one way they could earn enough money so they could live, and some of them didn t get that accomplished, so, but in that days there wasn t work for all of these people. It s like today, but, they had the big families and that way the children could help earn some money. : JO: George, when the family went to the beet fields, how much did they get paid? : GEORGE: They got paid by the acre, and it was from, at that time, from twenty two to thirty five dollars a acre, it depended, during the First World War they got up to thirty five dollars a acre, but before that and afterward they got back down to around twenty two or twenty four dollars a acre, and they used to kind of figure a family, ten acres per person, that is white people, Mexicans twelve, and Japanese fifteen, that s thev way, I heard the Great Western Company field superintendent make that statement one day, ‘cause I questioned him and he said there isn t too many where the family is like your family where they can ail. go out andwork. They have some little fellas that, were counting them too that shouldn t be working yet that are working. See most Japanese work with the short handled hoes, you called the thing, chop with one hand and thin with the other one, where white people they d use a long handled hoe and one hoes and one crawls behind it and thins, does the thinnin'. That s an act that very, very few white people learn to do, hoe with one hand and thin with the other hand, work both hands. I saw a fella one time, years ago, at the Liberty Theater, they used to have a live act show, twice a week, the first three days a week » and they had a fella in there, he was a dark complected fella from some island, and he worked alathe, you know a woadenlathe, and he worked one tool with his hands and one tool with his toes, and where he came from where they done wood work on lathes that s the way they were taught. JO: Well now, back in the beet fields when one of ‘em hoed did the other one come along thinningon their knees? GEORGE: Yes, on their knees, hands and knees. JO: The smaller kids, were they the ones thinning? GEORGE: Yes, they re the ones that done the thinning. JO: Did you do that? GEORGE: I done some of that and I done some of the other. JO: How did your knees hold up? GEORGE: That was bad, if they woulda just took, say two weeks or three weeks before they started thinnin' and woulda washed them knees with boric acid solution to toughen the skin, boric acid solution will do that, that woulda helped an awful lot, but NBCO, #004, page 19 GEORGE cont.: they didn t do it, seemed like nobody knew about aie JO: Probably didn t know about it then. GEORGE: Well, I don t know. JO: Then how long would you work? During the day. GEORGE: When it got light enough in the morning until it dark at night. JO: And the only time you stopped was to eat? GEORGE: That s right. JO: What would the meals be like, because. GEORGE: Well, that depended a lot of the woman, the mother. My mother done a pretty good job of cookin’ regardless, and, but my mother could do more work in one day than most women could do in two, anyhow. There was few women ever lived that could do as much work in one day as my mother could. JO: Well, what else about the beet fields can you tell us? GEORGE: Well... JO: How did you get out there? GEORGE: The railroad company on a certain day, the beet field company would have a, the sugar company would have a contract made with the railroad company that had, oh, maybe 25 coaches -and about that many boxcars, and you d have your baggage and furniture and everything all hauled over there and put in the boxcars and the next morning they d get into the passenger and toot off and away they d go for Western Nebraska. JO: How long did it take to get there? GEORGE: Well, you d leave here, get there about, usually about nine o clock the next morning, to Scottsbluff, usually. JO: So you spent near a whole day, a whole day and a night on the train? GEORGE: Yeah, it d take about 24 hours, see you d go to, from here to Alliance on a main line, the Burlington, and then‘ you d take that line into Scottsbluff. JO: Did you have to transfer? GEORGE: No, but off of the main line, see Scottsbluff ain t on the main line of the Burlington. JO: And then you got there and then what, how did you get to the field? : NBCO, #004, page 20 GEORGE: Well, the farmer d come in with a team of horses, team of mules, and load up your baggage and take you out, and you went out ten or twelve miles to, usually they didn t go twelve miles, ten miles or ten and a half would be about the limit. And you d be another day on the road. But the housing, that was pitiful. JO: What was it like? GEORGE: Just shanties, just, most people had better garages or better barns here in Lincoln than they had shacks out there for the people to live in. JO: And you stayed there from May to September, you say? GEORGE: From the middle of May to the middle of November. Now they got machinery that, uh, and the thinner works like, uh, radar works when a cop picks up a speeder, you know when he s parked with the radar, and the car flashes by, well that s the way the thinner works, it s the shadow off of the plant that makes the knife : but if it s a lump of dirt or a week, there s a still a shadow and the knife will . As far as I m concerned, that beet thinner isn t a success as far as I m concerned, and it s an expensive piece of machinery. Course, I was used to seeing beets worked by hand originally, and they ll never get me educated to seein' beets grow in bunches and two and three in a bunch, and JO: So how long did you do that? GEORGE: We went to the beet fields eight time. We went to beet fields when I was real little, four times, and four times after I was growed up: The last time we went the beet fields we just kinda went on a lark ‘cause the kids wanted to go more than the folks did. In 1923. JO: Well now, when you went on the train, where it took all day, how did you eat? GEORGE: You just made a lunch to last long enough ‘til ya got there. JO: What would the lunch be? GEORGE: Oh, whatever Mom would put up, my mother could put up a pretty good lunch. There d be homemade sausage usually, and some rye bread, and, no, my Mom could put up a pretty good lunch. But in those days and the way we were raised, we never had the variety of food like you have now days, nowhere near. ‘Cause we never had no refrigeration. JO: In the summer time you probably had a good variety. GEORGE: Oh yeah, well, we did in the winter time, too, the necessities, but not like they have now, like they have salads and things like that, you just didn t have ‘em in them days. JO: Well, George when you were out, when you down there at the beet fields and you were there early in the spring until late fall, could you put in a garden out there? NBCO, #004, page 21 GEORGE: Oh, yes, and usually we d set some hens and raise some chicks, usually. JO: Well, the garden, did your mother can anything? GEORGE: No, no, we never canned anything. We used to put up, my mother used to put up some dill pickes and them pickles and string beans in a crock. Now I ve told that to some people already and they ve never heard of it, but my mother used to pickle string beans in a crock. And they were good. ESTHER STURTZ: I ve heard of it, used to. sauerkraurt, my mother GEORGE: Yeah, my mother used to even, you know, pickle apples and, uh, oh, several other things in barrel. ESTHER STURTZ: Watermelons. GEORGE: Watermelons, they were good if they really, you get ‘em Ripe. ON, lOve ESTHER STURTZ: Pickled, you pickled the whole little round watermelon, about so big. GEORGE: A couple years my mother bought watermelons off of your dad when you was on the farm to pickle. Oh, my mother was a, she could cook and sew, my mother was a wonderful housekeeper. I had six sisters and she done all the sewin'. JO: Did your sisters, did your mother teach your sister how to do housekeepin' like he did? GEORGE: Yes, and, most of my sisters were outstandin' good housekeepers, most of ‘em. But it, it s like they say, you know, some get Americanized awful fast. JO: Well, some of them were born in America. Well, how old was your mother when she died? GEORGE: Seventy two. She was six years younger than my Dad, see when Mama died I bought the house over there on the corner where that lives and then Dad lived with me for six years, until he died. My wife s mother died in that house, too. She come to live with us and passed away there. JO: Well, can you tell us anymore about the beet fields? GEORGE: Oh, that was hard work. I always said that was honest money. Anything you earned in the beets, that was honest money, that was hard work. It still is, I think, even with the machinery they have, 'cause , you know they hadda plow deep , they hadda have exceptionally good soil, and they hadda cultivate deep and when you, in those days, when we went to beet fields it was all done with horses and it was heavy’ work for them and, and, it was just hard work from the day they started ‘til the day it was done, and a lot of them old fellas that farmed, they never did get out of debt. I don t know, I. . .Some of ‘em just wasn t businessmen NBCO, #004, page 22 GEORGE: cont.: enough to be farmers, they were goodfarmers but they wasn t businessmen enough to be farmers. They should have had a good bookkeeper to tell ‘em what was goin' on, ‘cause somebody else was doin' the paperwork, that s what I blamed a lot of it onto. Course a lot of 'em too, you know, just like would say last fall, them good feeder calves and white faced steer calves brought over a dollar a pound, right off of the cows, and they purtin near hadda double their weight before they was worth what they cost when ya bought 'em, ‘cause they got clear down to sixtysome dollars there once, they ain t much over sixty now, at calf. Well, they cost a hundred dollars a hundred pounds, a hundred and fifteen dollars they brought at Ogallala they brought at one sale was in the Nebraska Farmer, ‘cause you can t feed cattle that way and make anything. And a lot of them old fellas they fed cattle or sheep and that s what put ‘em under, too. JO: George, did your mother have any brothers or sisters? GEORGE: Oh, yes, had four brothers here in Lincoln. JO: Any of them still living? GEORGE: No, there was Uncle Adam and Uncle Henry and Uncle John and Uncle Fred. Lena Baker s dad was Uncle John, and John Schwindt, you know Katie, the white haired girl was her name, well, her dad, that was Uncle Adam. And Uncle Fred he moved out on a farm, oh, near Hastings, along about in 1922, that was her youngest brother. And Uncle Henry that Mrs. "st dad’, he lived in that third house from the corner down there from the Emmanuel Church, Reifschneider owns that house now I think. See Uncle John lived on the corner and Uncle Adam and then Uncle Henry, the three lived right there in a row. Uncle Fred lived in that house where Katherine lives and then when he went to the farm Uncle Adam bought it. JO: Your father, did he have any brothers and sisters? GEORGE: Yes, he had two brothers, they went back to , Germany. JQ: What: for? GEORGE: They didn t like it in Russia, and they went back to Germany, and he had one sister, married, she was older than my Dad, she married a man of the name of Schnell(?), and there was a group of people at that time went from Russia to Brazil and she went alons to Braziliand her one boy come to Lincoln one time, oh, after they d been doen there thirty some years and stopped to visit my Dad. He come to Lincoln and then had to go to Omaha, they bought the International Harvester dealership down there in Brazil, they farmed but they bought the dealership, and he stopped here in Lincoln. And then he had a sister that, she lived in Colorado, I never knew, got acquainted with her. There were more in that family, I just, right now off hand I can t tell you, but, uh, Dad was the only one that come to the United States. NBCO, #004, page 23 JO: Well now, did all of these brothers and sisters, did they get along all right, work together? GEORGE: No, when that break up came that the two went to ; Germany, that was a deal. . . you know, over in the Old Country, Russia passed a law they couldn t enforce it, uh, they couldn t work out, but when a man died his oldest boy fell heir to the debt, it he had any debt, the oldest boy fell heir to them, and that s where that break up come in at. Them two boys went to Germany. They had some, my Dad had some relatives there that never went to Russia, you know, when his grandparents or whoever it was went with that group, there was some that didn t go and they were Soil at , Germany, and, so they had their difficulties in those days already. But Russia never kept a promise in their life and they ain t gonna keep one now, I don t believe. When them people went over there to Russia, they were supposed to be a hundred years free of military services, they never kept that promise. They was all supposed to get a certain amount of land given to ‘em, like homesteads, that never was done, then they changed it it was just the male children, not the females, just the males. My Dad, yeah, one boy and six girls, some families you know had six or eight girls, well, females didn t count. But they never even lived up to that agreement. They ve never lived up to an agreement and I don t think they ever will, no matter what kind of an agreement you signed with Russia. When Hitler took over, the Jews went to Russia, and were promised a lot of ; and! they never kept them promises. JO: What kind of work did your father do in Russia? GEORGE: Oh, just, farm a little bit and what work you could get in between times is. . .They only farmed you know, a few acres, you know, one or two horses and then everything was done by hand, with a sythe and cradle and, you know, tromped it out, they didn t have no thrashin' machines or nothin' in them days, and it d be the work you could get and that didn t amount to nothin", and they never had enough to eat at any time, I don t think. JO: You said your father borrowed the money to come here. Who did he borrow the money from, who had that much money? GEORGE: LenaBaker s dad was in this country before my Dad was. He took one of my sister s hoes and he said, "Let s get goin'." Cause I was swingin' along, and then he stepped it off, you know, and he was doin' more than twice as much as I, and workin" half as hard. Boy, I just made up my mind, I can learn to do that. It s heed. toecet used to ic, but if you would do it riceht off the start, whoever starts you out, why, you could learn to do it. And he had a nephew with him, (Lenhart?) was his last name, that , that was that kid that got blew up in that potato cellar, you know, he went down there to get a sack of potatoes, and the farmer, shot a, he had a clothesline wire from the cave out, a big cave you know, you could drive in with wagons.
