Mr. John Kapeller, Jr. (008) Transcriptionist: Glenna Dorais Cumulative Record: July 9, 1981 2 00 3 00 10 6 45 7 45 liz 2 00 4 00 Total Time: 4 hours Total Pages: 16 NARRATOR S NAME: John Kapeller, Jr. TAPE NUMBER: 008 DATE OF INTERVIEW: June 30, 1980 PLACE OF INTERVIEW: 926 Claremont Street INTERVIEWER S NAME: Anna Baker FOR: North Bottoms Oral History Project ANNA BAKER: Would you tell me your name please? JOHN KAPELLER: Mr. John Kapeller, Jr. ANNA BAKER: When were you born? JOHN KAPELLER: August lst, 1908. ANNA BAKER: And where? JOHN KAPELLER: Denver, Colorado. ANNA: Who were your parents and where did they come from? JOHN: My parents, uh, my Dad s name was John Kapeller, and my mother s name was Dorothy. And my mother came from Russia and my Dad came from Germany over to this country. ANNA: Your mother came from where in Russia? JOHN: (Hook?) ANNA: (Hook?), Russia. Do you know when they came over? JOHN: Oh, about 1906. ANNA: And they lived where when they first arrived? JOHN: Well, they come here, down to the, uh, shall I call it the Bull Dog Ring? ANNA: All right. How many children were there in the family? JOHN: Two children, Martin and John. John was the oldest. ANNA: Only two children. Were there any born, no, your parents did not marry before they come over here. JOHN: No. ANNA: They married once they. . . JOHN: Married when they got over here in this country. ANNA: You attended. . . JOHN: Hayward School. ANNA: Hayward School and from there you went where. JOHN: From Hayward School I went to Whittier Junior High School. NBCO, #008, page 2 ANNA: And you are how old? JOHN: I m a be on August lst, I m 71 right now, I m gonna be 72 August lst ANNA: OK, and we re going to talk now about the area that is called the Bull Dog Ring. OK, tell me the area that is involved. JOHN: Well, that would be from uh, from A Street down to 7th Street, clear back to 6th Street, and that would be about four blocks, area there, and about, oh, I d say 25 families, be involved in that corner. Just a little corner there, I don t know where the name come from but I guess somebody started up because everybody had a dog at that time and I guess somebody says, well, that s a bull dog ring, that s where all the dogs go back there, barkin' and everybody couldn t get back there on account of the dogs. ANNA: Could you recall some of the names of families that lived there and their addresses? JOHN: Well, uh, there was Boswell Craig(?) he started on the corner on 8th Street, and then there was Philip ,» Conrad Carl Kildow, and then there was John Kapeller, and then later on way back there in the corner wasi ,» was an old man, he was a I don t know. . .And on the other side was John Willett, Alex Miller, Alex John Burbach, Henry Lowe, Sr., John » Eva Braim(?). that was a widow lady, she lived on the corner, and then there was a John Braim next house back, and then Wilhelm, and then across the street there was Conrad Lowes and then there was an empty lot, and then there was Henry Lowes, Jr., and then there was a Hock(?) and Phillip » And those are the families approximately round ne in that Bull Dog Ring. That many families. ANNA: Could you just tell me a little something about some of these people. JOHN: Oh, these were all poor people, they couldn t, uh, didn t have much to live on. They had, didn t have no inside toilets, they had outside toilets, and they had wooden sidewalks and they had pumps outside where they got their water, and had kerosene lamps at that time, uh, some of ‘em electric, I think, at that time, but there was a lot of, still lot of kerosene lamps around here at that time. And, we never had, we had to have ice brought in; you know, in your little ice box. You d have, uh, say 25 pound ice, .2 d have a card; and put on a window, and then the ice man would come along and give you ice for, uh, 25 pounder to put in your box, and that would be our refrigerator. And a lot of times, my mother would take our meat and put in the pump, we had an opening on the pump there where it would be cool in there, and we d put our meat down in there in the pump, underneath, uh, would be a ledge there and we d put that down there keep it cool. ANNA: What kind of meat was this and where was it made? \) NBCO,| #008, page 3 | JOHN: Well, I don t know, this come from Henry Maser, grocery store we traded with. They used to call it, at first it was a basket store, they used to call it, before it was, uh, Henry: Maser bought that basket store, and we used to trade by him, and that s where we d go down there, and we d take our little wagon, my brother and I, we d go downthere to Maser s and get our groceries. Mother d give us a slip of paper and we d take it down there and get our meats and fruit, whatever you needed. ANNA: Could you tell me exactly what kind of meat you hung down in this pump? JOHN: Well, I don t know, all different kinds, I suppose pork’: chops we had at that time, and I remember one time when I went to get the meat, I noticed on the corner of the package it was still wrapped up in the package, and there was a little hole in there, where the mice would be, uh, chewed on there and made a hole in thereto get after the meat. ANNA: Was this, would this also be the meat we called German sausage? JOHN: Yeah, yeah, could be German sausage also, yes. ANNA: Did your parents every make. . . JOHN: No, they never made their own sausage, no. ANNA: Not even out at the beet fields. JOHN: No. They never made it ‘cause my mother, uh, I guess, uh, I don t know, they just didn t get into that, the makin' sausage. But they was other people that did make sausage and they bought it from them, see. ANNA: The house your parents lived in in the North Bottoms, do you remember the address? JOHN: It was, uh, 720 W, no 720 Y. ANNA: Could you describe your house? JOHN: Well, it was a small house, there was, I think, there was only about, there was no basement, and it had two, little kitchen, and then it had I think two bedrooms, that s all. And a little bitty porch in the front. It wasn t very big at all. Just enough for three, four people tv live in. ANNA: Did this dwelling also have, what they call a summer house? JOHN: Yes, we had it, called it a (buck?) house or summer house whatever you want to call it, and that s where we, uh, they done their washing in there, and stuff like that, and mother would do, alb! her work in there. And storage, would be storage would be in there, and we had, in back of that, we had a chicken coop yet,- where we had our own chickens at that time yet. Chickens and ducks and stuff, we had, everybody had their own chickens at that time yet, back there. Some of 'em even had the hogs, I think. NBCO, #008, page 4 ANNA: Describe the area down there, about the streets, and again the sidewalks. JOHN: Well, the sidewalks were all, uh, they had wooden sidewalks, there was no cement sidewalks at that time, and they all had outside toilets and water pumps, and kerosene lamps, and everybody, in the streets there was no pavement in the streets, it was just mud. Everytime it rained, you d get stuck in the mud. And I knows lot of times, the grocery men, Maser s Grocery, a truck would come down there to delivery grocery to the people and they d get stuck down there and it d take 'em a long time to get back and lot of times, Maser, I don t know what his name was now, HenryHiegel, he used to come down and work for Maser and he come down there, and he d ask you in the mornings what you want for groceries. And then they delivered with this truck later on. And then you d order whatever groceries you wanted and he d go around house to house and pick up the grocery list and then they deliered later on. ANNA: Earlier, before we started taping this, you were telling me about an incident during the flood times between you and your brother. JOHN: Oh, yeah, well, lot of times they had flood over there and this here what they called the Bull Dog Ring was down in the low part of Lincoln and every time the, uh, I guess the Salt Creek would overflow and the water would come over to that part of town, and we d be in water all the time, we would have wooden sidewalks, naturally the wooden sidewalks wouldraise up and we as children would jump on these sidewalks and row, have these like little boats for ourselves. And it was fun playing around there. But my folks didn t think it was fun ‘cause then they hadda clean the house then afterwards. ANNA: Could you tell us anything else about any other families, what they did during the flood times? JOHN: Well, they all had to clean their houses ‘cause the water would get in. There were no basements under none of the houses, just maybe a little hole underneath where they d store stuff, you know, lot of times they had bootlegging in that time, too. And lot of times they d make their own beer at that time, and one neighbor would report the other neighbor if they was mad at each other, and report, you know, and then police would come down and they d throw the mash back out in the toilets or sometimes in the chicken coop and the chickens would get a hold of this mash and they would have, uh, wal. around like they was drunk, ‘cause they was eatin" this mash. And the police would come down, and well, they d get after 'em, you know, on account of makin’ their own beer or somethin' like that, which was prohibited at that time, you know, and they shouldn t have done it, but a lot of ‘em made their own whiskey at that time, not beer only, whiskey too, they had stills. But, uh, that s why they, one of, get mad at one neighbor, get mad at the other neighbor and they d report each other, see, and that wasn t too good. NBCO, #008, page 5 ANNA: Did your father make his own? JOHN: My father made the beer at that time, they didn t make no whiskey. But there was some of 'em made whiskey, but I don t want to mention any names whoever done that. "Cause they might get to hear this tape and they might get after me. ANNA: Did he have special utensils he used to make his own brew? JOHN: Well, yeah, they had their crocks and their bottler and I had to do the bottling. They d put the caps on the beer and they had the big bottles at that time. ANNA: After the beer was made, then what did your father do with it? JOHN: Well, sometimes they, well, we had a: little hole in the house, under the basement, under the floor, a little trap door, where they d go down and that s where they kept all the beer down there, and a lot of times they d bottle it, they didn t have a tester at that time, some of the families didn t have testers, and they d bottle it too soon and they d put it down in the basement, and I know we done that one time, and it, and during the night it started poppin'. All the bottles broke down there, ‘cause there was too much gas, too much power in there. So, a lot of times it happened that the bottles all broke, they d test, should have been three days or a little longer, see you d have to test ‘er when it was ready and that was the time it could be bottled. ANNA: Let s get back to the area called the Bull Dog Ring for a little while now again. Tell me, what did you, what did the kids in this area do for entertainment? JOHN: Well, they went, uh, there was a light post there on 7th Street, across the street from Carl Kildow, and from Henry Lowes right on the corner of Henry Lowes s house, and the children would go over to that corner there and they d play games like hide and go seek, somethin’ like that, they d play games and play under this lamp post, that s all the recreation they had at that time. No buildings to go to, in the evenings they just played under that lamp post until about nine o clock and then they had to get inside, 'cause the parents was after ‘em, they wouldn t stay out there: longer n nine o clock, that was their limit. ANNA: There was a German version of the baseball came way back then, I believe it was called Matka(?). Can you describe how... -. JOHN: Oh, yeah, matka. Well, I didn t, I don t know too much about that there game that they played baseball. I didn t play baseball at that time. I didn t play with them at that time. That must have been after my time or before my time, I don t know. ANNA: The men that lived in the Bull Dog Ring. Could you tell me what they did for a living? NBCO, #008, page 6 JOHN: Well, some of them they went to the beet fields, and some of ‘em worked on the railroad. ANNA: Did you and your family ever go to the beet fields? JOHN: Yes, we went to the beet fields around, uh, 1930, I think around there, '31, '32, we went to Baird, Nebraska, we went to the beet fields, and I think it was two or three years that we went to the beet fields. ANNA: When you went to the beet fields, from what time of the year to what time of the year were you gone? JOHN: Well, that was from May, I think that s when they started, out there to thin the beets, in the different towns, it was Baird, Mitchell and all them different little towns out west of Nebraska, and they d leave here in Lincoln, they d have those boxcars here in Lincoln, under the 10th Street viaduct. GAP, TAPE STOPPED? ANNA: Could you tell us from when to when you went to the beet fields? JOHN: Well, it was around 1930, '31, '32, went to Baird, Nebraska, and wentout there to, uh, Erhart, I think was the farmer s name, and we worked beets out there. I don t know how many acres, it was 30. acres or so that we worked that year. ANNA: From what month to what month were you gone? JOHN: Oh, that would be from May to October or around there. And tell us about what your parents had to do before you started on your trip to Baird as far as getting the . JOHN: Well, we hadda move our things that we wanted for out there, we hadda move it into a little, uh, they had boxcars along the track under the 10th Street viaduct, and the people would move their furniture, their tables and chais and stuff like that, what they d need, just, uh, the main things that they ould live on out there in the beet fields, they d move that into the boxcars and then they delivered out here, different towns, like Gering, and Baird, and Mitchell and all different towns, every car would be a different location. ANNA: The house that you lived in once you got to the beet fields. . . JOHN: We had this, just a little shack, it s like a little bigger than a garage or somethin' like that, just a little one room shack. And you d just have your beds there and your, you just made your own kitchen there in that little shack, just enough to, live in to eat and sleep and go to work in the morning, every morning 'til you had your job done and workin" in the beets. NBCO, #008, page 7 ANNA: What time would you start working in the beet fields? JOHN: Real early in the morning. ANNA: ‘Til when? JOHN: "Til late in night, 'til you couldn t see, you had to, we put in maybe 12, 14 hours every day, and the folks would use the hoe for hoeing and thinning and the children usually would crawl on the ground and do the thinning, and they would, uh, sometimes they would leave, supposed to leave only one beet standing, lots of times they left doubles and then the children got scolding for it for leavin' the doubles and then they hadda go back over it again and get that other beet out. They s supposed to have and a lot of times the children would take: and put somethin’ around their knees so their knees wouldn t get so sore. I know mine would, got awful sore. And then, uh, we d put kind of rags around our knees so they wouldn t, protect ‘em a little bit and then when we got too tired then we d make the folks go down and get on their knees and we took the hoes. ANNA: And one you did all the hoeing and then what was the next step? JOHN: Well, then the next step was to go through and first, uh, weeding, you know, to pull out the weeds, and second time and third time, you know, they d cultivate, you know, and then get some of them but they wouldn t get all of the weeds around the beets, and we d have to go through that and get the weeds out of there. And then around the fall, when they was up, ready, then we hadda top ‘em. ANNA: What do you mean by topping? JOHN: Well, they had a puller from that farmer that pulled the beets and raised them up out of the grounds and then you d have ob take ‘em and hit ‘em, take two beets and hit 'em together and throw ‘em on a pile, and you d go down this whole row. like that there and throw em on a pile and then you had a big pile of ‘em, then you d move down further and then, and make another pile, just keep on doing that through all that, and then later on you d top these piles, you take beets and you d have a knife and you d take and uh, you d have, uh, a big point would be on that knife and you picked that beet up and put it on your knee and chop all that green stuff off and then you d throw that beet on another pile where they d come later on and picked these up with a fork, farmer would come along and have beet forks, and they d throw them in the wagons and then they would haul them to the beet dump. ANNA: And then what was the final step? JOHN: Well, that would be made into sugar, the beets would be made, later onithey d go to the factory and they d be made into sugar, you d have your sugar from them. And lot of times when we had our beets all topped, in the evening, you know, during September, [ctober, around there, it would freeze, and then we d take the beet tops and put them on top of the beets so they wouldn t NBCO, #008, page 8 JOHN cont.: freeze during the night, so next day if the beet was froze then it wouldn t be no good, so we put beet tops on there. ANNA: John, knowing the year is now 1980, many years ago you started a project, would you tell us everything you can about the project that you have done? JOHN: Well, I m thinkin' about the time when I was living in 1918, ‘19, '20, around that time, when we was livin', I was a child yet, back there in, what they called the Bull Dog Ring and I was thinkin' about it one day and then, that was in the year 1975 and I think, well, why shouldn t I make somethin' that I can remember the rest of my life where I lived one time? And I started that project of a little board and made little houses and put each, uh, and made individual, a little lot of each family, marked it on a litle board, and that was in March 6, 1975, when I made that. ANNA: Well, how long did it take you to make the project? JOHN: Oh. . .About five or six hours. I made a board, cut a board and then just pasted the paper on there and then drawed the lots on there and put them people s names on there. ANNA: Did you have any help in doing this? JOHN: No, I done this all myself. ANNA: Could you, by looking at it now, would you sort of describe other things than just the houses. JOHN: Well, uh, this was called the Bull Dog Ring and, uh, one place on the west end of this here, uh, Bull Dog Ring, they called, where these houses was, was a Crab Lake, and we used to go back there and take a little summer sausage and put it on the end of a string and put it in the water in this Crab Lake and we d catch, uh, little crawdads, and we d take them home and a lot of times we d even eat them, because there was little crawdads, and the tails of them crawdads were good and we used ‘em a lot of times #o) go fishing. And this Bull Dog Ring, from 7th Street up to 8th Street went uphill and the tracks were on the south side, railroad tracks, Burlington Railroad tracks, and there was a alley and, uh, on the north side there was just nothin' but a empty field, and on 8th Street there was Mr. Burbach, and Mr. lived on 8th Street, to the east. ANNA: Would you just give us some of the addresses of these different places? JOHN: Well, I haven t got no addresses, no address of any of ‘em, just, uh, there s four families were living on, uh, between 8th and 7th Street, and there was about three families livin' from 7th Street to 6th Street, and then the rest of 'em all lived from 6th to 7th on the south side, to 8th Street, there was about ten or 12 families on that side of the street. But this has all been taken away since the Interstate went through, took all this whole corner out and there s some other building is back there now and this land is all gone, these houses. NBCO, #008, page 9 ANNA: When the houses disappeared because of this overpass or part of the Interstate, what actually happaned to these houses? JOHN: Well, they just took 'em and burned ‘em, uh, lit a fire to 'em. Didn t even tear ‘em down, lot of 'em, just burned 'em down. ® ANNA: Were some of these houses moved to other places? JOHN: No, not that I know of. I can t remember of any houses being taken away from back there, ‘cause they was so old, 50, 60, 70, 80 years old these houses, it was 1928 when we got there, these houses were old houses already at that time, 1918, so I don t know when these houses were built, were started, but they was old. ANNA: As far as you know now in the area that was once known as the Bull Dog Ring, there are no houses there or anything at all. JOHN: No houses back there at all no more, nothing back there no more. And we lived back, from, 1960 the Interstate went through and took all these houses, and a lot of these people had to look for different places, go different places and buy homes, and where they got very little money for their homes, what the Interstate took there. And we left there in 1960 and we come to 926 Claremont here on 9th Street and we bought our house here. ANNA: Knowing you live down here in the area called the North Bottoms to this day, what do you think people thought about the city or the State putting in the Interstate? JOHN: Well, they didn t like it at first, all these people had to move and look for different houses and that was kinda hard and they didn t have the money to go and buy, the houses were higher at that time, see, these little houses what they had at first, they got that for, just for nothing, just about, say for a thousand or two thousand dollars they boght these little homes, and then they hadda go out of these houses and leave, and, uh, go get a house maybe ten or fifteen thousand, which is pretty hard, and they hadda go into debt and that was kind of hard for a lot of these people. ANNA: You know a lot of these German Russian people who still live on North 8th Street. Have you talked to them about the Interstate and what their opinion is? JOHN: Oh, well, I talked to the Burbachs over there, they re the only ones left yet over there, Jake Burbach lives there and I think their son now has got the place of their dad s, their dad and their mother are both gone, and the boys got the place yet, that s the only house yet close to the Bull Dog Ring, that s the only house that s one 8th Street there yet ANNA: Has he ever told you what he thinks about... JOHN: Well, he don t like that Interstate either, ‘cause he has to look at a mountain on the west side of him, and on the NBCO, #008, page 10 JOHN cont.: east side, well, there s a paint shop back there, paint shop and he s the only one on that corner now, that Burbach boy. ANNA: Could you tell us, are there any old timers that still live back there now like they did when they. JOHN: Not, not, Mrs. (Firestein?), she just died about, uh, about six months ago and she was about the oe one of the old timer that lived back there, Mrs. ANNA: And she, do you know whereshe lived at back there? JOHN: Well, she lived on 8th Street, on the, on the southeast corner of 8th Street there. I couldn t tell you the address. ANNA: Could you tell me about how old she was? JOHN: The house is still standing and she was over 80 years old, ‘way over 80, I think she was 85 when she died. But the house~ is still there yet and her daughter s got that house now. ANNA: And where s, a man who owned a great deal of property on the west side of North 7th Street, would you know who this man was? JOHN: Oh, this wasTravelinski(?), he was, uh, I think he was a Jew, I think he was, wasn t he, or no, he was, uh, a Polack, wasn t he, Polish? I don t know, but his name was Travelinski and he had all that land back there on, uh, from the, what they called the Bull Ring, north up to that Bull Dog Ring. He had had all that land back there. Travelinski. ANNA: From time to time, I have talked to kids who have now grown up into adulthood and they have talked about snow ball fights that they used to have back in what they called Travelinski s pasture END OF SIDE A ANNA: Could you tell me about how much you were paid to do this work in the beet fields? JOHN: Well, I couldn t exactly, can t remember right now what we got paid. I think it was, uh, for the whole job of them 30 acres, I think it was around three thousand dollars that year, for that whole, all that work, all that time we was over there. And then when we come back that year and we would have enough money to buy another little house a little bit better house than where we lived in the Bull Dog Ring, we moved up to 8th Street and bought, my folks they bought a little better house up there, at that time, and houses were real cheap that time, you know, two or three thousand dollars you could buy a house. ANNA: Was the money used for ings purposes besides buying the better houses once you came back JOHN: Oh, yes, you had to have money for food and clothing, and NBCO, #008, page 11 JOHN cont.: all this. ANNA: Were you children paid a salary? JOHN: No. We worked for our folks, we hadda work for them, we d make a livin", all four of us work together, my brother and I and my folks, we worked to make a living, to make ends meet. That s where, otherwise the children, the folks wouldn t be able to live at that time in the Depression time, with just one, my Dad workin" alone, this way there was three others, working helping making that money, make a living, to get a start. ANNA: When you were working out in the beet fields, did you, what did you do about lunch? JOHN: Well, we would, uh, this little shack, beet shack what we had, was right by the land where we was workin' the beets, so when somebody got hungry, or, one or ‘em, mother would say go back to the shack, get some water or get somethin' to eat, and then we d sit under, maybe there was a tree there, and we d sit in the shade and have our lunch and then start in again. We wouldn t have to take an hour lunch, we d just eat a little bit and then go again, start workin’. ANNA: What did you eat for lunch? JOHN: Well, we had sandwiches and fruit, whatever fruit that we had at home, what we got in the grocery stores during' the day, a lot of times we d go to Baird, we had a Model T Ford at that time, and, uh, we d drive that into town on Saturday night and we d load up, buy enough groceries Saturday night for the whole week. We figured, my folks they figured out how much they d need for that whole week, and next Saturday night, they d go back into Baird again and buy groceries again for the next week, that s the way we operated. From one week to another. ANNA: How far was the little house from the town? JOHN: From Baird? Oh, I d say 15, 20 miles. ANNA: And your father and mother would leave on what day of the week to go do grocery shoppin? JOHN: On Saturdays, Saturday evening we would go in, say Saturday evening, we wouldn t work too long on Saturday in the afternoon then we got home to the shack, and then we d take the Model T Ford and go to Baird and get the gruceries, folks would. ANNA: And this grocery consisted of what? JOHN: Oh, meat, and fruit of all kinds. ANNA: The German Russian people, women, were noted for their baking. JOHN: Yeah, my Mother done baking too, yes. NBCO, #008, page 12 ANNA: What things did she bake? Could you describe. . JOHN: Well, she baked rye bread, and then she baked, uh, baked pies, like other women do, and, uh, cakes, she d do all the bakin', yes. ANNA: Were there any original German dishes, pastry or something she would make? : JOHN: Well, I d have to say it in German and you wouldn t understand it. There d be and there would be that s noodles and would be potatoes in it and bread would be on top of, toasted bread would be on top of that. And there would be, uh, they call that ,» that d be German sausage they had once in a while, but I can t remember havin’ that in the beet fields, "cause we could get that, see, that was, uh, when we got here in Lincoln then we had that here in Lincoln. ANNA: Would you tell us. in English what was? JOHN: Well, in English would be, uh, it d be sauerkraut and mashed potatoes, you put the sauerkraut on top of the mashed potatoes, and you d have some pork with that and that would be your meal, that would be a German meal. ANNA: Was this sauerkraut bought or made? JOHN: Well, it was bought most of the time. ‘Some people they made their own sauerkraut, too, some of the German people, but my folks I don t think, I can t remember them makin" sauerkraut, because we just needed a little bit for one meal, you know, so that s all they d use it for. ANNA: When you came back from the beet fields, how did you get back and what did you have to do in order to get back to Lincoln? JOHN: Well, we d drive our little Model T Ford back, it d take us quite a while, I don t know how many days from, it was only from Baird to Lincoln, that was only maybe 450 miles, 400 and some miles, but it d take you a long time ‘cause you d go 25 miles an hour in that there, we had that Model T all full of stuff and the folks would sit in the back and my brother and I would sit in the front and we d do the driving. And they d load us up again, the boxcar, they d take our furniture what we had, a table and chair and beds, back to Lincoln again and then we d have to move that back into our house again when we got back to Lincoln. ANNA: The clothing like suits and dresses and this type of clothing and towels and things, what did you put those in? JOHN: Well, they would be, uh, we wouldn t have too much of that, towels and suits, every, I d have one suit and my brother would have one suit, we wouldn t have two or three suits at that time. And my folks even wouldn t have many suits at that time either. ANNA: Did your parents have something called a trunk? NBCO, #008, page 13 | JOHN: Yes, they had a trunk. And that s where they would keep their bedding stuffin there, their pillows and their blankets and stuff like that, in the trunk. Some of them would call them the hump back trunks, you know, the kind of a round top on 'em and some were flat, too, trunks. And that s where they put most of their stuff in there, they didn t have no cedar chests or somethin’ like that at that time. ANNA: When you were working in the beet fields, I have been told about the farmer and his horse which drug this wooden working tool Behind it. Could you tell us about this? JOHN: Well, he would, uh, in the fall when they worked the beets, they d have two horses and they d use either a lifter, it would be a lifter for the fall for to pick up the beets and it would go through and it would pick the beets right up and raise it up out of the ground and then we d have to take the beets and pound ‘em together to get the dirt off of 'em and throw ‘em on piles. The farmer, he would lift ‘em out of the ground first. ANNA: When you were at the beet fields, besides working in the fields, did you also have a garden of your own? JOHN: Yes, we had a little garden of our own, and we had mushmelon and canteloupe and stuff. And right ‘side that little house that we had, that little shack, we would dig a hole, be sandy soil, we d dig a little hole, and we d put our mushmelons down in that ground, because we didn t have no refrigerator, didn t have no ice and nothing, no ice man didn t come around at that time, so we just dug a little hole and put their mushmelons and fruit down in this little hole, which would be cool and damp, and we d put a little board across the top so it d keep cool down in there and that s where we kept it for a few more days instead of spoiling. Otherwise it was spoiled. ANNA: When you were leaving the beet fields to come back to Lincoln, and there was food left over, what happened to that? JOHN: Well, we took that along with us in the car. We ate it as we went along from town to town, we had our food and we ate there that way, Sandwiches and stuff. ANNA: Did you have to go school while you were out in the beet fields? . JOHN: No, no school. A lot of times when you left here in Iincoln, we hadda miss school, a few weeks before school was out even and that was, the teachers didn t like that ‘cause we was leavin’ before our time and we had, I don t know, some of the children had to make the time up later on in the fall, I guess, the time they lost before spring, it was a couple of weeks before school was even out, ‘cause that was in May when we left here and school didn t go out, I think, until June, wasn t it, June, isn t it, school was out, that s about three weeks before. NBCO, #008, page 14 ANNA: When you lived in Lincoln, then at the time you lived here in Lincoln, and growing up, would you tell me a little bit abour your childhood? JOHN: Well, growin' up in Lincoln here, my folks they, my Mother especially, she was always goin' to prayer meetings, and she loved the prayer meetings and she took us boys to the prayer meetings and we d have to go along with her, all the time, if you liked it or didn t like it, we had to go along, and we d sit on benches and a lot of times when the men would be talkin' about the Word of God, we d fall asleep, ‘cause we was little and we wasn t interested in what they was saying, and we hadda go along with my folks, listen to the prayer meetings. And I went to prayer meetings, from my seven years on, ‘til, uh, I m goin' to prayer meetings yet, ‘til the prayer meetings stopped here in our church, and that s better, uh, 60 years, I ve been goin' to prayer meetings. ANNA: What is a prayer meeting? JOHN: A prayer meeting is, uh, where, uh, men and women come together and they re religious people, they believe in God, they believe on the Holy Bible, and they believe, and we d have sometimes two men talk about the Bible. They d get a few verses out of the Bible, they d read it, and then they ll speak about the Word of God. And then they d sing songs out of the it s a book, a song book, and the book. There d be two books there they would sing out of and they loved to sing the German people, the German Russian people, at the prayer meeting, they loved to sing. That was their main thing after they got through preaching the Word of God, and then they d pray, all of ‘em would pray, and then they would sing songs, they would sing a few songs, then they would pray, and then they would sing a few more songs, and then they d pray again. And this would go on for two hours. And it would be on Wednesdays, at seven to nine, and then on Saturdays, seven to nine, Sunday afternoon, two to four, and Sunday night from seven to nine again. Four times a week they d have prayer meetings. ‘Til later on, it got weaker and weaker, less people come to prayer meetings and then they cut out the Wednesdays, then they finally at out the Saturdays, then they finally had the Sunday evening cut out, then finally they cut everything out ‘cause there was nobody left, it just died away, praying. In 1972 or eto the prayer meetings died out at the Emmanuel Reform Church in Lincoln, Nebraska. ANNA: Were these prayer meetings held in churches only? JOHN: Yes, well, at first, they was held in the houses, in, well they call ‘em summer kitchens, they would, different places, like Mr. (Schwendt s house or Mr. Gerlach s house, house they d call ‘em, little summer houses, they would be people in there, and when that got too big, too small, then Reverend said why don t you stay out of the housesand come to the church and we fixed the church basement up and we used to stay in the church and have their prayer meetings. And that s where we stayed in the church for all them years. NBCO, #008, page 15 ANNA: At these prayer meetings, did the minister also. .. JOHN: He would come there once in a while, yes, and he would preach to 'em, they let him preach, and select the Word of God, whatever he wanted first, then he would preach first, then a couple brothers would talk, too, over the same Word, and then they d have the same thing, the singin' and praying again. ANNA: Can you talk German real good JOHN: Yes, I can talk German. ANNA: Knowing that the German Russian people loved to sing at the prayer meetings, would you without music sing a song for us in German? JOHN: I d have to go and get a book first and remember the words a little better. ANNA: All right, why don t you do that then. PAUSE: ANNA: John Kapeller now will sing a few songs out of a German song book which is called JOHN: The book, the book, and it s number 8 in the book and the song is 6 JOHN SINGS JOHN: And, uh, I ll sing out of number 7, out of the same book, and the song is JOHN SINGS ANNA: John, you told me that a friend of yours had a favorite song. pig And that s Mrs. (Fink?) , she liked this same book, number 306. ANNA: Weuld you sing that song? JOHN: Well, I don t know if I can sane that song or not, I ll have to look for it. ANNA: How old would Mrs. Fink be at this time? JOHN: Oh, she would be about 90. ANNA: When you were growing up, did you sing German songs, church songs at your home? JOHN: My mother, yeah, she would sing the German songs at home and we d have to listen to 'em as children, and they took us to the prayer meeting and we had to listen to the songs there, they sang. They had two books, they had the . book and the NBCO, #008, page 16 JOHN cont.: book, two books. ANNA: Was there a certain time of the week that you would sing German songs? JOHN: Well, that d be Wednesdays, Saturdays and Sundays, would be the time, when we had the prayer meetings. ANNA: I see. Outside of that you would not sing. . . JOHN: Well, in the evenings, lot of times, where, we was talkin' about the Bull Dog Ring, we d go, I know my folks would go over to Finks or Millers and sit on their porch and they would sing these songs. In the evening. Out of the book or the book, one of em would start in singin' and they would sing it without notes, no music or nothing in it, and they would sing a lot of times, uh, for an hour or so, sit and just, sit on the porch and sing songs. And this is Mrs. Fink s, was 306, (reading the German words of the song?) That s her song. ANNA: John, could you tell us, if you know why and how these people became known as German Russians? JOHN: Well, I wouldn t know how they, that come from Russia END OF TAPE

ANNA: No, Uncle John had talked to (Stroh he was the ticket agent and he sent the tickets over, Stroh did. But Uncle John stood good for it, paid him back. ANNA: Well, there was a lady and then, uh, a child died, but I didn t see the lady, but I found out, well, we was goin' up to go up on the deck and the sailors we d ask ‘em how long it took and such as that, and anyway, this lady and her husband they were tendin' people sittin' there cryin' and I went over and I says, "What is the matter?" "Oh," she says, “You ll see pretty soon, ‘and my — baby died and they were gonna bury it here," and I says, "Ok" and I stood there and kinda comforted her for a while and they took that baby and, they had it tied on a board, and then they had a rope on that board and they had a stone on the other end and they opened a door in the bottom of the ship and let it down there. GERTRUDE: There was a big hole in the bottom of the ship is that what you mean? ANNA: ee that they could close up you know. GERTRUDE: And they just threw that baby in there. JOHN: No, no, at that, when I, around here they changed it, you just, this was only sixth grade down here and then you went to junior high. MOLLY: And then to high school. JOHN: Yeah. MOLLY: Could you speak German in school at all, or did you try? JOHN: Oh, no, you might have spoke to your friends in German, you know, if you wanted to, but, well, it was pretty much English, and our parents wanted us to, they wanted you to talk German at home, but in school and that they wanted you to learn the English language, they insisted on it, and your teachers did, too. MOLLY: _Do you recall any problems during the war with being German? Like say the first World War or second World War? JOHN: No, I was, I was just born in 1914 but my parents, yeah, they had, they couldn t talk German or anything around people, they, people d get nasty, lot of places they, well, they weren t exactly barred, but they knew there was trouble if they went there so they just stayed away from it. MOLLY: Did they ever say anything about German foods, like say sauerkraut, not being offered in stores anymore or being called different names? JOHN: No, no, , but they maie their own sauerkraut so they... MOLLY: What about the churches down here, do you recall the names of the churches and where they were located? JOHN: Oh, yes, Reformed Emmanuel which is Emmanuel now, is a church my Dad helped build and which I d gone to, get confirmed in, got baptized in, confirmed in, married in. Yeah, then there was St. John s, well matter of fact, two St. John s churches down here, at that time, one was on 10th and NBCO, #010, page 17 JOHN cont.: New Hampshire and the other was, well, it s still, ,» New Hampshire, about US the GERTIE: 14th. JOHN: *14th? And then Faith over here, that was ‘the name - Salem, yeah. MOLLY: Do you know why people belong to the various churches, how they would decide which church to belong to? JOHN:, Well, it was, like I said the village they come from, uh, they more or less stayed in the same churches . GERTIE: Wasn t there a church over there on, uh, 9th and... JOHN: Well, yeah, church right over here where the on the corner of 9th Street, uh, 9th and Y over here, at one time, but I don t remember the. . .. MOLLY: What other villages were people from down here aside from Norka? JOHN: Oh, uh, » and (Hoock?) _, ; F oh, let s see, I can t remember ‘em, ' T guess, well, there s several more but I just can t think of ‘em right now. MOLLY: So people were primarily from along the Volga River? JOHN: Yeah, around, uh, and that area, along the Volga River, some of ‘em worked right in ; worked for some mill workers and things like that. MOLLY: What sort of wedding did you have when you got married? JOHN: We, just, church wedding, just a little church reception, uh, well, we had it at the Welfare, just a small reception. MOLLY: You didn t have a wedding then? JOHN: No, no, we, well, my brothers , Gert s father s house » no we didn t have a big wedding. MOLLY: Have you ever attendeda wedding? JOHN: Oh, lots of ‘em, lots of ‘em. MOLLY: Were you ever at any of these so called three day dance weddings? JOHN: Oh, yes, yes, it was quite a deal, we used to shivaree all those weddings there, kids, and those, oh, this was quite a deal, I mean, they, they their meals, roasts, and, uh, supper, breakfast, they had the whole works, it was a lot of work, it took a lot of, a lot of women ; and they danced hard, and they d be soakin' wet. H] NBCO, #010, page 18 | MOLLY: Is that something that you think they brought over from Russia? JOHN: Oh, yeah, yeah, this was, was the custom over there. MOLLY: Were these usually over at the Welfare House? JOHN: No, there was a lot of tents, rent a big tent, dance floor, and big tents, and they d set 'em up in, oh, backyards, some of just set ‘em up in the backyard and then they d cook in the basement, drag the food out you know. MOLLY: You said there were lots of shivarees, did you ever participate in any of those? JOHN: Oh, yes. MOLLY: What did you do? JOHN: Well, you just get and cans and then hollered and bellered and made enough noise until they finally come out and then they d give you some money and get the hell out, get out of here. MOLLY: About how much money would you get. . « JOHN: Oh, you probably got, if there was eight, ten, twelve kids then you got ten, fifteen cents apiece, and, well paid. MOLLY: Did you have any so called gangs down here, like boys did they have gangs? JOHN: Oh, yeah, yeah, purtin' near every area, like 14th Street had theirs, we had ours here in the 10th Street area, the Bull Dog Ring had theirs, oh, yeah, there was, you know, sports, football and that MOLLY: What sort of games did you play? JOHN: Well, you d play football, uh, baseball, softball, you know, and, uh, and then you ae uh, what' d they call that game where you marked the sidewalk . MOLLY: ach JOHN: Well, we played » yeah, but this here. . .chalked the sidewalk where you was gonna go and hide, you know, just, oh, yeah, it ll take, sometimes it d be dark, you know, and they d still be lookin' for you, and lot of times you sneak home, see, MOLLY: It isn t fox and geese is it, or. . .I don t know how you play that, but I ve heard the name of it. NBCO, #010, page 19 JOHN: Yeah, well, we just, we used to say start it here you have to stay here, oh, maybe ten minutes and the other team they go out and scatter out, you know, and then you d mark and then they would follow, follow the arrows and try to find you, see. And then tiffy(?), oh yeah, tiffy(?) was big fall game, winter game. MOLLY: Can you tell me how you played tiffy(?)? JOHN: Yeah, you had, uh, what we did, with broomsticks and had two points, took a broomstick, oh, probably four or five inches, and we sharpened each end, and then you took a broomstick and you sharpened the other end and you hit that tiffy, went flyin' up in the air, and then we d mark off so many steps and you could credit, number, so many steps you got so much credit then, you played, uh, block, block long and block back, and then whoever had the most, the shortest between the block was the winner, , Lot of windows broke. MOLLY: Do you know why it was played in the fall and. the winter more than. . . JOHN: Well, there wasn t much of anything else you could do then, you know, it was too cold, too chilly to play outdoor games, this here kept you warm. MOLLY: Do you remember matka(?)? JOHN: Matka(?) ball, oh, yes, yeah, used to, this was I think just made out of a sock stuffed with rags and stuff, that was the only ball you had, you know, and you d sew it up, your mother sew and sew and you d take ‘em home, and then you d knock hell out of ‘em next day. And, oh, yeah, then later on we got a soft ball and we got older ones that schools wouldn t use anymore and things like that. MOLLY: Can you tell me how you played matka? JOHN: Well, just like, uh, baseball here, you got up and you batted, and you had the bases, and you hit the ball and run your bases back and you was, uh, you batted again and you just kept this up, wasn t much skill or anything to it, just a matter of who hit the best. MOLLY: Did your family ever work the beet fields?. JOHN: Yeah. MOLLY: Do you know when they started working the fields? JOHN: You mean what year? Oh, they must have started, uh, let s see, must have started around, uh, oh, I think 1910, 8, 10 in there somewheres. MOLLY: So, did they start as soon as they got here or did they wait awhile? NBCO, #010, page 20 JOHN: Uh, no, they worked around awhile, and then my Dad worked with the railroad for quite a while, and then later on they went to the beetfields, there, kids grown up and nobody to help ‘em, my older brother and sisters. MOLLY: So you did work the beet fields? JOHN: Yeah, I had a couple years of it. MOLLY: How old were you? JOHN: Uh, eight. MOLLY: And, how did you get to the beetfields from Lincoln? JOHN: Train. MOLLY: Where did you catch the train? JOHN: Right, right here, right here at the tracks right across the street here, under the viaduct here. MOLLY: Approximately how long was the ride to your destination? JOHN: Oh, it probably took, uh, generally into Scottsbluff and areas, most of the people went, up to ten, ten, eleven hours. MOLLY: Then did you stay in western Nebraska? JOHN: Yes, there and Minatare. MOLLY: How did you prepare for your trip out to the beetfields? JOHN: Uh, had big bexes, what they called beet boxes, but they was like, well, like we would know trunks today, but they was homemade built, homemade, everything went into it, dishes, clothing, and, uh, all that went into these boxes, and then, it was what you, necessary things was, and then when you got there, why you bought whatever you needed. MOLLY: What did you do on the train while you were goin' out? JOHN: Just set and looked out the window and chewed seeds. MOLLY: What? What are Rooshen seeds? JOHN: Sunflower seeds. MOLLY: Did you chew very many of ‘em? JOHN: Oh, the floor would be, of the train, would be three or four inches thick. MOLLY: Who got to clean out the train then? JOHN: Train people. NBCO, #010, page 21 MOLLY: Did you ride in a box car, regular pullman car. JOHN: No, coaches. MOLLY: So you did have seats and everything. JOHN: Oh, yeah. MOLLY: How did you find out who to work for? JOHN: Uh, they had, uh, the factories, sugar factories out there that sent, had a man here in Lincoln that would have contracts. They would get the contracts, factories would have farmer, contracts with the farmers, to raise the beets, and then they d have their man here goin' around and gettin’ people to work, sign the contract to do the work. MOLLY: Were there people other than German Russians that worked the fields? JOHN: it was, uh, oh, therewas some Mexicans that was out that area "that worked, 5 MOLLY: What time of year did you go out and what time did you come back? JOHN: Well, you generally left, uh, in April, in April sometime and then you d be back, try to be back by Thanksgiving. MOLLY: What was the progression of the work you would do, like when you first got out there what did you do, and then through the summer. . . JOHN: Well, you, the first thing you did, well the. number first thing you did when you got out there was to buy a pig, butcher it, fry the meat down and pour the lard over it, Then you went into thinning and blocking the beets, that s, you had, someone would hoe and then you would out, you would leave the best beet and you d space ‘em, space the beets, so you had one single beet there and another one down, and then after that you had to, what they called the hoeing, then you had to go » you had about three hoeings during the summer, keep the weeds down, and then in the fall you d, uh, top ‘em. But durin' the summer like my Dad and my older brother they would stack hay, help the farmer, stack hay, this was all extra money, uh, irrigating, to do the irrigating for ‘em, regular ferm work. — END OF SIDE B MOLLY: What sort of homes did you live in when you were out there? JOHN: Well, the one, one we lived in a regular house, the one year was ,» and the other one was what they called beet shacks, it was just, oh, just a roof and the walls, windows and doors, and it was, a shack. NBCO, #010, page 22 MOLLY: So were the accomodations out there less desireable than the homes you lived in? JOHN: Oh, yeah, much, outside of the one, the regular farmhouse we lived in there, but the others, yeah, they were, was warm and wasn t as cool in the summer. MOLLY: What was the average size of the beet field, like how many acres? JOHN: Well, like, uh, the years we worked 'em, I think we worked uh, 70 acres one year and 80 acres another year. Uh, we helped some of the neighbors a couple a times, just a few acres, but we, it was a family that we had there, we worked around 70, 80 acres. MOLLY: So your family alone worked that many acres? JOHN: Yeah. MOLLY: Now would that mean that a farmer would maybe have more land that other people would work? JOHN: Oh, yeah, well, it couldbe or that s all the beets that he would have and the rest of it would be in hay and grain. MOLLY: What sort of foods did you eat when you were living out west and working the fields? JOHN: Oh, we, regular meals, meat potatoes, » rye bread, ‘ MOLLY: Any particular German Russian foods? JOHN: Ah, no, not really much different. MOLLY: Did that differ much from when you lived in Lincoln? JOHN: Oh, no. MOLLY: You just didn t eat many German Russian foods at all? JOHN: Oh, yeah, but, I mean, we ate about the same out there as we did at home, only thing is that there the meat they had to fry it down because there was no refrigeration or ice in those days we cid get fresh meat once in a while, we d go to town’ to the grocery store and get it, you know. MOLLY: What did you do for entertainment when you weren t working? JOHN: Just little fishin' or somethin' like that, that was about the size of it, wasn t too much time for that. MOLLY: Who took care of your homes in Lincoln when you were out there? NBCO, #010, page 23 JOHN: Uh, generally, well, I had an older sister that stayed here and then she, they just boarded 'em, most of ‘em just boarded ‘em up took off. And the amazing part if you done that today, you know, you got back you wouldn t have anything, but you d come back and everything would be in order. MOLLY: How long was the average work day? When did it start and when did it end? JOHN: Well, you d work practically sun up to sun down. MOLLY: And, did you get breaks during the day? JOHN: Oh, yeah, you had your lunch time and ten o clock lunch, you had to eat ‘cause you worked hard. MOLLY: Was it hard work? JOHN: Oh, yeah. MOLLY: About how difficult would you say comparing it to what you ve done the other part of your life on other jobs? JOHN: Well, the hard part about it was that most of it was bending over and the heat, terrible, hot summers, uh, it was, uh, winter time, then it d be cold and frost bitten fingers, toppin' the beets and that, but, uh, it, it, was hard work, but I suppose we ve done harder work other times. But this here you had to keep goin' all the time because first you had to get those beets thinned so they wouldn t grow too big before you get through them and then keep he weeds out, and you just continuously had to go. And then in the fall when they was ready to harvest you had to keep going keep from, uh, first freeze come along, why it d freeze the beets, heavy frost come. So you just continually kept workin’. MOLLY: What was done with the beets after they were harvested? JOHN: They was hauled into the sugar factory, beet factory there. MOLLY: So that was in Nebraska then? JOHN: Yeah. MOLLY: Did you miss much school by being out in the beet fields? JOHN: Yeah, yeah, you see, you d, well, I d say out of every three years of school you d probably lose a year, MOLLY: How did you do that, say if you came back in November, did you go right to school then and just try to make up what you missed? JOHN: Yeah, or they d have, uh, set back, uh, they would have a class where as you d go back and try to get caught up first before you joined your regular class. NBCO, #010, page 24 MOLLY: Do you know how you were paid or how much you were paid in the family? JOHN: Well, you were paid by the, by the acre, uh, roughly I think about, the lowest I remember was about $13 an acre, and uh, then you also, you got a bonus, if your beets weighed so much you got an extra bonus, so in other words, the neater work you did, the better work you did, the more you d get paid, you go by tonnage, and the beets would run all the way from 10 to 20, 21 ‘ so if you got up around that 20 ton you got a pretty good bonus, uh, and then like I said you got, make extra money, my older brother and Dad would do farm work for the farmer and get paid so much a day for doin” it. MOLLY: Was it considered good pay to work in the beet fields? JOHN: Uh, yes, uh, if you, uh, if you could work quite a few acres which also depended on the farm the ground you was farmin' on, some ground couldn t, they couldn t raise dust let alone beets, you run onto a farm like that you just didn t make much money, but the average live all winter on it then. : MOLLY: How did it feel to have to do such hard work for produce that wasn t even your own, land that wasn t even anything that belonged to you? Did it bother you at all, or was the money enough incentive? JOHN: No, yeah. Evidently it was, you know, I mean, as far as, what I can remember back, folks was contented and like I said they probably saved money : MOLLY: Why did your family stop working the beets? JOHN: Well, the family, the older brothers and them, they just got out on their own and the family got smaller, it was a family affair to go to the beet fields, involved the family, if you didn t have a big family you didn t make much. MOLLY: What sort of work if any did your father do in the winter when you weren t working the fields? JOHN: He worked, uh, for the Northwestern Iron and Metal Company when we come back in the winter, they always had a job there, and then he went into the garden business after that. MOLLY: Where was Northwest Iron and Metal? JOHN: It was right under the 10th Street viaduct, where, uh, the parking lot is, the baseball diamond and that, that was all Northwestern Iron and Metal. MOLLY: What sort of jobs have you held since then? JOHN: Well, I ve worked for the railroad, I ve, well, first I worked for this Travelinsky there makin' horse radish and workin’ on the vegetable farm. And, uh, railroad, worked for Nebraska NBCO, #010, page 25 JOHN cont.: Neon, uh, worked for lumber, worked, uh, in the drug store first drug store that was open was » I got three dollars a week there. I was about 14, I think, 13 or 14. Yeah, and then I went and bought my own garbage route and then I was in the garbage business for nine years, and then I bought a tavern andI run that years and then I built a liquor store out in Havelock and was in there for 16 years. MOLLY: Can you tell me anything about when you worked for Mr. Travelinsky, with the horse radish? I mean, what did you do? JOHN: Well, we d, uh, first we done the same thing as you, kept the weeds down and everything, grow it up and then you d harvest it, you had a big cave, filled this thing with horse radish and carrots and potatoes, two big caves, then you took the horse radish, you d have a potato, uh, what they called a potato peeler, but it was just a big cement, it was like a washing machine, it was a big rough cement inside, and you would put water and the horse radish in there and this would, uh, circle it and it d clean the horse radish off, you know, that s what they got took the peeling off potatoes, and then we ground it, we ground the horse radish and then you put it in big jars, salt it, vinegar it and salt it, and you let it set for a couple of days and then you d bottle it. Clean your head out! MOLLY: “here did he market that horse radish? JOHN: Uh, wholesale Saeed outlet in Omaha, Raymond Brothers, Grangers, (H. B Law?), all them here, and then restaurants would buy them gallon jugs, hotels, restaurants, buy the gallon jugs, it was bottled and labeled, uh, I think we labeled for about eight or ten wholesale houses. It was all the same horse radish, but each, uh, each company would have their own labels, out of Omaha bought truck loads of ‘em. MOLLY: He had this entire operation down here in the North Bottoms? JOHN: Yeah, yeah, just an old, little shack. MOLLY: Where did he raise the horse radish? JOHN: Out, uh, where the Interstate and all that comes in, that ground in there was along the railroad, why they would lease it to him for practically nothing, to more or less keep the weeds down. Raised horse radish there, carrots, tomatoes, a lot of tomatoes, uh, potatoes. MOLLY: How long did you work for him? JOHN: Oh, I must have worked for him three or four years, I was a kid. MOLLY: So that primarily summer work then? JOHN: Yeah, yeah, well, winter we d, we d make horse radish all winter long, in spurts, you know, you d get so many orders NBCO, #010, page 26 JOHN cont.: in, why, he d let us know MOLLY: Was it pretty strong horse radish? JOHN: Oh, yeah, it was the best, really, lot of it straight horse radish, nothin’ added, outside of vinegar and salt. MOLLY: Let me see, you worked at the drug store also? JOHN: Yeah, for a while there, yeah, about, MOLLY: What did you do there? JOHN: Just kind of an errand boy, flunky. MOLLY: Was it Winter Drug when you worked there? JOHN: No, it was, uh, Barth, yeah, it was the first drug store in the Bottoms, full drug store. MOLLY: Were the Barth s German Russian? JOHN: Uh, no. MOLLY: What about the Winter s, are they German Russian? JOHN: No. MOLLY: Did that bother people at all when outsiders came in that had businesses? JOHN: No, not when they, when these people started comin' in. Barth, a whole lot of people knew Barth because he run the one on South 9th, the drug store, for years and year, and he, he was quite a, purtin' near a veterinarian, you might say, because with all the animals people had, chickens and that, they go out there and tell ‘em what was the matter, he d have pills or whatever, so, he was quite a man. MOLLY: Did they ever have a soda fountain up there? JOHN: Yeah. MOLLY: Was that quite a few years back? JOHN: Oh, yeah, well, it must be 42, 44 years ago. MOLLY: Has it always been in that location? JOHN: No, this was over here by the beauty shop, was where he started, Barth did, yeah. MOLLY: Oh, so moved across the streetithen. JOHN: Yeah, they moved over, then he sold out to this, uh, I think, was his brother in law or son in law, brother in law I believe, name of Yost, he bought it then. And then later on, uh, who bought it from Yost, and then Winter come in after that. NBCO, #010, page 27 MOLLY: One thing I forgot to ask you earlier was about the German school. You had mentioned that you went to Hayward and then you went to German School also. Now, was that like confirmation school? JOHN: Yeah, that was Sunday School, confirmation school, yeah. MOLLY: And how often did you meet? JOHN: Uh, well, you went twice a week, uh, you went, uh, oh sometimes during theweek after school and then on Saturday mornings. And also your regular Sunday School on Sunday. MOLLY: Was that all religious instruction? JOHN: Yes. MOLLY: And did they emphasize the German language? JOHN: Oh, yes. MOLLY: So did you learn how to write it also? JOHN: Uh, somewhat, yeah, somewhat, but you, uh, wrote in the well they called it » which would be American, uh, sound and the German, the German sound and the American letter, uh, alphabet. MOLLY: So, did you ever learn to read or write German script? JOHN: No, I never did, my Dad could do it real well, my uncles » L never c MOLLY: And you called this other thing 2 JOHN: Yeah. END

MOLLY: How would you get to town when you went downtown? CONRAD: Walked. Walked up and walked back. MOLLY: Did you ever take the streetcar? CONRAD: That cost money and we never had no money. MOLLY: Never rode it once in your life? CONRAD: Well, we d jump on it and ride it. Without payin', yeah. MOLLY: Where did the streetcar run down here, what streets did it go on? CONRAD: Well, it came down, uh, 10th Street and then go down to Charleston or New Hampshire, and , then, uh, I think it went outto 14th and turned around and went back, back the same way. Andwe used to, uh, ride it in the wintertime, we d, with our sleds and wagons we d hook onto it. MOLLY: Sounds kind of dangerous. CONRAD: Well, we, it was fun, though. NBCO, #013, page 11 MOLLY: Did anybody ever get hurt doing that? CONRAD: No, not that I know of, not, uh, not that I know of. MOLLY: Do you recall anybody taking the trolley off the streetcars so that. . . CONRAD: That, we d do that, too. MOLLY: Did you ever get in trouble for that? CONRAD: No, we d run. No, we used to get a big stick and get that, that arm and run it off, then the guy would have to get out and put it on, and we kept him busy. MOLLY: Do you recall any rivalry between South Bottoms and North Bottoms? CONRAD: No, I don t, not too much, I mean I ve heard of a lot of ‘em when they d get up like the middle of the viaduct and that d be about, be a big fence here where you couldn t get through unless you wanted a fight, and, uh, I don t remember, I ve heard of it, but, and then down South Lincoln the same way, and if youwent down South and you got in trouble, I was fortunate I had two brothers married girls from down there and they, they knew me, and I could go in anytime I d want to and they wouldn t bother me. MOLLY: Do you have any idea why there was any fighting between North and South? CONRAD: Well, the only thing I knew of, they didn t want them people down there to come get our girls down here, and we didn t, they didn t want us to go down there and get their girls. That s the only thing I can figure out. MOLLY: So it was just over women, huh? CONRAD: Well, yeah, they still fight over ‘em. MOLLY: What do you recall about this neighborhood as far as appearances went? Like if you would be walking down New Hampshire or Y Street or any of those streets, when you were growing up, what would you have seen? CONRAD: Well, I would seen one of the nicest, cleanest neighborhoods’ you e er laid eyes on. There was nothing out of place, there was no junk layin' around, and it was clean, everybody kept their yards clean, painted, and wintertime when the snow fell, as the snow would fall and you d see some of them old folks out there shoveling snow, right in the snow, and the minute it quit, it wouldn t be too much longer all the streets would be clean. There wasn t nothin’, no snow on the streets at all, you could walk any place. MOLLY: Were the streets paved. CONRAD: No, not the streets weren t paved, they were gravel. NBCO, #013, page 12 CONRAD cont.: Now the street I lived on, it was cindered, nothin’ but cinders 'til, way until after I was 20 years old. MOLLY: What sort of sidewalks did they have? CONRAD: They had cement sidewalks. Some of ‘em, and there was a few that had board, board walks, but, uh, but that was soon put in concrete. MOLLY: Did most of the people have their yards fenced? CONRAD: Yeah, they had, uh, wooden, uh, they had a lot of ‘em had, uh, like hedge around it or wooden fence, picket fence, and, uh, or building brick, that was about all that they had. MOLLY: What would you say has changed the most in this neighborhood? CONRAD: Well, what s changed the most is, I think people that owned the houses here and, uh, that they handed their houses down to their children or sold it somebody and then they rented their property out and that s the only changes, and now a lot of it s rented out and it s not like it used to be. And then hard times, I mean we re livin' we did then. MOLLY: Do you like the neighborhood now as well as when you were growing up? CONRAD: Uh, well, I like it just as good now, yeah, but some of this you gotta just overlook because you gotta change with it. MOLLY: If you could make the decision and make the neighborhood like it used to be where everything was clean and all the people owned their homes and things like that, would you do it? Or would you keep it the way it is? CONRAD: I would do it, I d like to see it back like that except if we could have everything else, I mean, I wouldn t want to go back to that, but as far as havin' it clean, yes, that s, what I like. MOLLY: So are you living in this neighborhood because that s where you really want to live? CONRAD: neighborhood. MOLLY: Do you think this neighborhood has something to offer that perhaps some of the other neighborhhods in Lincoln don t have? CONRAD: Well, no, I think all neighborhoods are the same, except I know what it s » what it s been and I can walk down the street today and there s no street down there that I don t know maybe 50 percent of the people, and I d say the other 50 percent is maybe rentals or some of their offsprings that you don t know, you don t see anymore. MOLLY: Now you had said that your family work beetfields. Did you go along when they went? NBCO, #013, page 13 CONRAD: I started when I was eight years old, and I worked until I was 16, and all my other brothers were older than I was and then they married and then there was only, uh, two of us at home and we didn t go back to the beetfields, but they would go every years and I worked in 'em just, just like anybody else did. MOLLY: Why did your family choose to work beets? CONRAD: Well, that s the only income they could have and then at that time we couldn’ t, uh, buy a job, there wasn t too many jobs available and some body with a lot of kids like that needed somethin' and needed it quick, where everybody could work, and, uh, we d go out every year and I think we made a pretty good livin' with it. We had all the clothes we wanted and everything that we wanted to eat, we didn t starve or, was in any bread lines that I know of. MOLLY: How did you get the jobs out there? CONRAD: Well, there was a gentleman down here by the Johns, Fred Johns and he, he would get contract with, uh, different areas out west and, uh, they would write him letters tellin' that he needs a family that can take care of maybe 50, 60, 80 or a hundred acres of beets and then he d go around to these families that he knew that had that many kids that d take care of so many acres and then he d tell ‘em, now do you want this job, I got it for you, look the situation over and I suppose that s the way they got it. And they d have to have a little old shanty for us, shack, what we called ‘em, beet shack, and sometimes it d be three rooms, and we d all sleep in it, in that three rooms, just just one big bed. MOLLY: How did your family prepare for the trip to the beetfields? CONRAD: Well, they put everything in big wooden boxes, they d be Maybe three by six box, wooden box, and then they d nail it shut and it had hinges on it, and they d put all our clothes in it, and uh, these, uh, beet growers would, uh, send a train down and everybody, certain day and this train would take ‘em to their destination, and, uh, they d dump ‘em off and they get to ride the train out there, and the beet growers would pay for the transportation. Except for later years, we had our own transportation or somebody that, one farmer would maybe have a truck and he d come in and say well, we don t need ya until a certain time, and then he d come in with a truck and load everything on the truck, and move out to his place and start to work. And that s the way we went until we got done and “hen we d come back to Lincoln MOLLY: Now, did those trains just have cars full of people going to the beetfields, there weren t any freight trains or anything like that. CONRAD: No, no, just, uh, well, like maybe what you d call boxcars or somethin' for their baggage. MOLLY: Were all the people German Russian? CONRAD: All of ‘em were German Russians, yeah, every one down there, yeah, well, NBCO, #013, page 14 MOLLY: So were there people from the South Bottoms also on those trains? CONRAD: Well, yeah, they was, they come down, as far as I know and they d get on the trains, yeah. MOLLY: What did you do while you were on the train? CONRAD: Just look out the window, ‘cause it usually took, we had to sit still, couldn t run around, but it was usually it took most of the time just one day of traveling or, or at night, because we used to get out of school at 3 15 and, uh, they said the train would leave like 4 30 and they left us go to school until that time and they would wait for us and they d be loaded, wait for our family down there at the train and we d jump on it and take off, then at night, next day we d be where we wanted to be. MOLLY: Did you ever eat sunflower seeds on the train? CONRAD: Oh, yeah, we, everybody had a pocketful of them. MOLLY: Did the floors ever get very full of the shells? CONRAD: Oh, yeah, you d walk along and hear ‘em crackin’. MOLLY: Then once you got to the beetfields, what was the first thing your family did? CONRAD: Well, they d have to make their, like we couldn t carry no mattress or anything so we had to take mattress covers and fill them full of straw, wheat straw or whatever it was, and that was our mattress, and then we just, uh, prepare ourselves for, for the beets, so, uh, start workin' on ‘em, and that was usually about maybe two weeks after we got there, we d thin 'em, that would take all the way from four to six, six weeks to do that. And there was always somethin" to do, we d either be in the beets or puttin' up hay or shocking grain or irrigatin' or whatever, pickin' potatoes, and that lasted until beet harvest and right after that, when we got done it d be just a matter of a few days and we d pack up and leave. MOLLY: How many hours a day did you work? CONRAD: Well, from, uh, sunup to sundown. MOLLY: So you put in a pretty long day. CONRAD: We was puttin' in a long day. MOLLY: Was it pretty hard work? CONRAD: Real hard, real hard. MOLLY: How did you feel being a little child doing work like that? CONRAD: Well, we didn t know any different, I mean there was no, no feelings to us, I mean we knew that we had to do it, we didn t know anything else. We couldn t say well, I wanna do this or do that. That s all we knew how to do. NBCO, #013, page 15 MOLLY: Do you know how much your family got paid? CONRAD: I don t have any idea what we got paid. MOLLY: So approximately how many months out of the year were you gone to the fields? CONRAD: Well, it d be a lee May, June, July, August, September, October, and November. ight months. MOLLY: And then you d take a train back to Lincoln? CONRAD: Take a train back, or later part of the year, later part maybe drive the car back. MOLLY: Now who took care of your house here in Lincoln while you were gone? CONRAD: Well, usually a neighbor took care of it, or one of my brothers would maybe come back to Lincoln or they had one brother or somethin’ that stayed here in Lincoln that was married and didn t go out, he d maybe go over and mow the lawn, and they d have boards they d nail over the windows to keep somebody from knockin" out a window or somethin’, they d nail it shut and lock it up, shut the water off and electricity and that s all of the, didn t have gas then. MOLLY: Approximately what percentage of the families that lived down here went to the beetfields? CONRAD: Oh. .. I d say maybe 45 percent. MOLLY: Did you ever talk to anybody that stayed here in the summer to know what it was like? CONRAD: Oh, yeah, all my buddies they didn t go, well, they just said it was just empty, but it was, as long as they had one or two friends to run around with that was about it. MOLLY: Do you know if there was any vandalism in the summer with that many houses empty? CONRAD: No, I don t think there was house busted in or nothir.'. I don t remember our house ever broke in, and, uh, on the street I lived in there was, uh, two, four, six, eight, ten, ten houses, and out of the ten houses there was, uh, one, two, three, four, five, six, six of ‘em, uh, went to the beetfields, and I don t think none of ‘em had anything broken. MOLLY: Do you remember specifically what communities you went to when you worked the beetfields? CONRAD: Well, it varied, we went out to Cozad, ee eri we went to, uh, Scottsblurr, Minatare, Baird, and ’ Wyoming, and we went to Sheridan, Wyoming, and for several years in uh, Mitchell, Nebraska, and we worked four years I know at Cozad, Nebraska. NBCO, #013, page 16 MOLLY: Was there an area you like working better than any of the others? CONRAD: No, because you got, you got acquainted with your friends, uh, after you got there, and then maybe the next year you wanted to go back and you didn t go back and then you get acquainted with somebody else, it was just always, always the same, except if you were fortunate enough to go back to the same place and then you d, uh, you d meet your old friends back then that you had seen before, and maybe they moved out or somethin' like that. MOLLY: Why did your family stop working the beets? CONRAD: Why? Because the family grew up, married off and there was only two of us left and we couldn t, couldn t do it anymore. MOLLY: So, once you didn t have a large family anymore it was hard to do something like that. CONRAD: Yeah, you couldn t go out and work, work bh the fields because you went out there and somebody would happen to be sick and there was only three of you workin" or two of you and then there wasn t, uh, you couldn t, you couldn t do it, the beets have to be tended at the right time or if not you d loose it. MOLLY: So you said you were 16 when you stopped working the fields? Then what did you do after that? CONRAD: Nothin’. MOLLY: Didn t work at all? CONRAD: Well, I, I worked on WPA for about, uh, three years, but I, and then I went in the Service when I was 21 years old and I was in the Service for five years, and then after, uh, after I got back from the Service I worked for company for about a year and a half, and then after that, I worked for, uh, for about two years and then for about 30 years. MOLLY: What kind of work did you do for WPA? CONRAD: Oh, we, we did dirt work, I mean cleanin' ditches or dig ditches or sewers. MOLLY: How old were you when you got married? CONRAD: I was 24, MOLLY: And who did you marry? CONRAD: MOLLY: How do you spell that last name? CONRAD# 2, U, By G, Be NBCO, #013, page 17 MOLLY: And was she German Russian also? CONRAD: Well, she s German, yeah, but she s not from around here. MOLLY: “ow did you meet? CONRAD: Oh, I met her when I come home from the Army one time, or i oat her. I knew her sister and then I met her through her MOLLY: Did you get married in one of the churches down here? CONRAD: No, we, uh, I was in the Service at the time and I come home on a furlough and we got married in a little town in Kansas. MOLLY: So did you have a dance wedding or anything like that? CONRAD: No, never had time. MOLLY: Did any of your friends have dance weddings? CONRAD: You mean since, when I ve been married? MOLLY; Well, anytime before or after or just anybody you might know that had a dance wedding. CONRAD: Oh, yeah, they all had dance weddings, I mean not all of ‘em, but there were a lot of ‘em had dance weddings, got married down here at the Welfare House MOLLY: Did you ever attend any of the three day weddings? CONRAD: No, I haven t ever, no, I had, uh, one of my cousins had a three day wedding but I never had the chance to go to that one beca Wyoming, MOLLY: Did you ever participate in any shivarees? CONRAD: Yeah, yeah, we used to shivaree, and then we wouldn t quit until they give us a couple dollars and then we d quit.

LOU WINTER: He, uh, started the drugstore in June of the year when he graduated from the University and that, uh, he had not passed the State boards at that time but he needed a job and couldn t find a job so he got this, a chance to buy this, and we sot the money from some of his relatives to buy the store, and then he took the State Boards a couple of months after he, uh, after he had been in the store. And it was really a one man operation, you worked from eight o clock in the morning until it was time to close at night and he worked all day every day for a long time. JO MILLER: In other words, he bought the store in June and didn t graduate until later and while he worked at the store he still went Go school. LOU WINTER: Oh, he was all through school. School was over but he had not taken his State Boards, he still had to take his State Boards, but they allowed him to do that ‘cause the State Boards, you know, you have to wait and take those at a certain time, so he did do he did get that. JO MILLER: And he bought the store from whom? LOU WINTER: From Mr. Campbell. JO MILLER: How long did Mr. Campbell have it? LOU WINTER: I don t know how long he had it, but he d had it several, oh, five years maybe or ten, I think he had it quite a while. And he went, he bought a different store in town. Mr. Campbell did.
