LOU: Well, he did, uh, he did everything, he was, opened it up and worked there all day long until it was time to close, we didn t have any closing hours really, we just kept, he kept working until there weren t any people around, so in those days you didn t have hours, you just worked. And then after he kind of built up his business a little more then he would get a student maybe to come in and let him go home for his meals and then he d come back and work again and very seldome did he ever get home 'til after ten o clock at night. H NBCO, #015, page 2 LOU cont.: And, uh, he worked that every, that was week after week, and we didn t have a vacation for 18 years, he worked without a vacation. JO: Can you describe the store for us? LOU: Well, at first it was, uh, sort of a L shaped store, and in the back part was the prescriptions and there was tables and chairs for serving ice cream, ‘cause we did have a fountain. And, uh, we had that for, I don t know how many years until, and there was a barber shop close by, next door, and, uh, Frank wanted to enlarge the store a little bit so they decided to, the barber should leave and Frank took over that area so, which made it a little bigger so we could have a few gift things. When they took over the, uh, barbershop, enlarged it enough so that we could handle more merchanise. We had a few gift items and more school supplies and oh, a few extra things like that, which we needed, and then in later years we bought a ice creammaking machine and put that in and we made ice cream there for many years and we had, uh, a Mrs. Horn came helped us make ice cream part of the time, and Betty, uh, oh, let s see, Betty, what was her name. . JO: Which Mrs. Horn? LOU: She lived just not too far from the drugstore. Bertha Horn. She made ice cream for a long time. And, uh, I made it, too, part of thetime I did that, and that was, uh, that was a good thing, and people would come in and want that soft ice cream in their ice cream cones whenever they knew we were making it. They liked it soft. And, uh, George, uh, (Geering?) used to come in almost every day to get sodas, he s, uh, he was a soda eater, and he always did that. And, oh, let s see what else about that. I don t know, can t thing of anything else now. Anyway, it was a good store for us, and Frank always enjoyed working there, and he dways enjoyed the people. He just. JO: Did Frank ever relate any unusual incidents or amusing stories or anything like that from the people? LOU: Oh, I m sure there were many of them, but I sure don t remember any of ‘em, but there were just lots of ‘em, and he enjoyed those people very much, and he was very happy, happy to be there. JO: Because now Frank did, did Frank have any German background at all? LOU: He was, came from a German family, but he really didn t know much German, much German but he could understand a little bit. JO: Well, then as he camedown here in this community, did he lear any German? LOU: Oh, he, they used to talk it, yes they did, he would talk, uh, say different, different words especially that he had learned and they wuld use ‘em and he came to be able to understand the: people quite well, but he, he didn t speak German, but he could make out what they needed, what they wanted. MOLLIE MAUL: My parents were Catherine Bauer, she came from Russia, she married my Father, Jacob Lebsock, in Russia, and they came right over to America, because he would have been drafted into the Russian Army and he would have been gone two years, and to avoid draft they came right to America after they were married. MOLLY COLLINS: What part of Russia were they from? MOLLIE MAUL: Frank, Russia. MOLLY COLLINS: And is that along the Volga River? MOLLIE MAUL: Right. MOLLY: Did they say anything else about life in Russiaas far as their reasons for leaving? Like anything about the conditions. MOLLIE: Oh, yes, often times, uh, my Mother would, uh, Father, also would speak, Father would go out and have, uh, they would go out in the morning with the entire family to do like gardening or if they had an orchard to pick trees or to make hay, and, uh, they would cook their noon meal and if they were working late at night they would have some left over for the evening meal, and I know they often spoke about the apples being picked and the strawberries being picked, and they were ripe at the time and it was sweet as sugar, you never ever had to use sugar. MOLLY: You think they were just recalling things better than they really were because they were homesick or did you have the feeling that that s the way. . MOLLIE: No, I don t think that they over exaggerated at all, I think it was, uh, absolutely just like that. MOLLY: Did they seem to enjoy their life in Russia? MOLLIE: Very much, very much, they enjoyed their life, and, uh, their earlier years in America must have been very lonely and homesick for wanting to go back, but they never did go back, then, uh, all we children were born, they had nine and we moved from one place to another, eventually moved to Lincoln. MOLLY: So, you think perhaps that if they wouldn t have had the fear of being drafted they would have stayed there but that was really the only reason they came over here. MOLLIE: Right, that s for sure. MOLLY: Where did they come when they first came to the United States? NBCO, #018, page 2 MOLLIE: Now, that I don t know exactly, I have no idea. It seems to me. . .they, they must have gone to Kansas because Jake, who was the oldest son, and, uh, they had this oldest boy Jake the first year they were married, so they must have gone right to Kansas ‘cause he was born in Otis, Kansas. MOLLY: Do you know if they came through Texas or through New York when they landed? MOLLIE: Well, they had to come through New York. MOLLY: Did they say anything about the voyage over, how they got here, or the name of their ship or anything like that? MOLLIE: No, no, I never knew that, they did say it, you know, now you can come over on a ship but it just takes two or three days or whatever it is, but it almost took them a week and of course a grandma, my Mother would, uh, say often how sick she was, she couldn t even get out of bed because the voyage made her ill. MOLLY: Did they say if when they left Russia they took a ship right away or did they take a train through Europe and then catch a ship like in London. MOLLIE: Well, I remember my Mother saying that her mother stood at the shore when they left on the ship, and, uh, had on an apron like they do and picked up the apron and was crying bitterly because she said good bye and that they probably wouldn t ever see ‘em again, so they must have been right close by. Not to my knowledge did they take a train. They might have gone some miles, maybe on a wagon and horse, you know, drawn by horses or something, now that I don t remember exactly. MOLLY: So did your parents leave a good number of family members behind in Russia? MOLLIE: Well, my Mother had four sisters and one brother, and the brother was the very youngest of the family. MOLLY: And none of them ever came to the United States? MOLLIE: Not the sisters, but two of, uh, my mother s one sister had two daughters and they came to America. Now to my knowledge, one is still living in Wisconsin, but the other, she and her husband are not living anymore. Their name was Strasheim. MOLLY: So, your mother s parents and her brother and sisters actually stayed over in Russia. Do you know what ever happened to them? MOLLIE: Well, they all died a natural death, but when the, uh, the Communist came and went to my, uh, uncle, my uncle s house, that s my mother s brother who was the baby of the family, the only boy, he inherited the brick home that they had in Frank, Russia, and they came and ordered them all out of the house, with only theclothes they had on their backs, and they took my mother s brother away and they never ever saw him again, took him to a NBCO, #018, page 3 MOLLIE cont.: concentration camp like they did, and they had to work and if they didn t keep up their work, the amount of work that they were told to do per day, why, they would whip 'em of whatever it would be. But as far as I remember as a young girl, it was on Christmas Eve, when Mama received a message that her brother died in the concentration camp in Russia. He never ever got to see his family again or any of his children or anything. MOLLY: So was he actually in Siberia in the concentration camp? MOLLIE: Right. MOLLY: Did your mother ever receive any letters or communication from him? MOLLY COLLINS: Do you know which villages they came from? MARIE SCHMIDT: Well, Dad come from Kukas and Mama come from (Stall?), wherever that is, but that wasn t far from where Dad lived, from Kukas. Cause they had certain lines that they traveled by, they can t go anywhere on that ocean. So the captain got everybody out on deck, and they got their boats all ready, and they got down and prayed, and then they sang a song or hymn, and finally they got far enough away from it so it passed the ship. And they took a picture of it. They had given the people pictures of it and I wonder what happened to ours. There was a machine that took the picture and the measurement above the water and below the water. Well, I think they aid it was a couple hundred feet or so above the water, it looked like a church, with steeples you know, like a cathedral. They said three quarters of it was below the water and one quarter above. Boy, that s where we lost time then, they had to get off of their route and then to get back again. We was on that same route, the northern route, that the Titannic sunk on. And that s what scared everybody. Sitting with the Captain when it was all over and he said, "Now, we ll have to thank God that we gettin' near 2 He wasn t all there, he didn t worry, he understood that Dad knew him, and I think he was from our home town. Anyhow, Dad talked to him, he was standin' at the railin' watching it, he says "That hits here, he said to God, you know what I m gonna do?" He says, "You ain t gonna do anything. He said, "I m gonna get right on there and ride back to the old country." Then we got the news later, before we got to New York » I don t remember where at, a burg hit short, it hit some harbor an just knifed the harbor and everything, and that was in the harbor, that iceburg. Oh, it was quite an experience. And them sailors, that was, up and down, one would come down, the other one up that ladder to that crow s nest with that guy sittin! up there and watchin' things and givin' the orders. They didn t have radios and telephones. Just one up and the other one coming down, that was half the night and all fore noon, 'til it was all over. MOLLY: What was the trip like, itself, as far as youraccomodations, HENRY: Oh, it was good. We come over c plenty of food. The accomodations weren t so damn good 1% was just like haulin' cattle, that is from the NBCO, #025, page 9 HENRY conic.> to the, Glascow, across the North Sea. It was just bunks, Sawdust scattered all over, people gettin! sick. We had some Jews there, boy you could hear them bellerin' all the time, seasick. And when we got there, we had a nice clean Ship comin' over. Each one had their separate rooms and everything. I% was an English ship. It was really clean and everything. nice people. It was pretty and real nice in England. When you listen to some of these that come by way of Germany, oh boy, that was terrible there, the way they were treated. In England there, we was treated real nice, couldn t complain. MOLLY : How did you communicate with those people? HENRY: Oh, they all had somebody to talk the language. MOLLY: But you couldn t speak any English at that point. HENRY: No, no, ; when we landed in Liverpool there was a man right there at the depot, talked to 'em, took the whole bunch. I remember that, that was at night. There was center of the street and he took the lead and marched us to the hotel, it was quite a ways, hold up his hand and at Fawcett Square stopped all traffic until we was by, took us to the hotel and then they fed us, showed us to our peds and everything. They were really nice, them people, couldn t complain. I d listened to some of them that come by way of Germany they had a heck of a time with them Germans. MOLLY: Were there all sorts of people on the ship? Different backgrounds, or was everybody Germans, or HENRY: Oh, well, I don t know. I know there was a bunch of Jews with us, and then there was, well that s when most of them German people come over here, was in 1912, from that war. That s when most of 'em come. That s about all there was, was Germans on there then some Jews. MOLLY: So when you first came over, you went to Wisconsin. HENRY: Yeah, Wausau, Wisconsin. MOLLY: Was that where your sisters were living? HENRY: Yeah. MOLLY: And then how long did you live there? HENRY: Lived there until 1916, come out here and been out here ever since. MOLLY: What sort of work did your parents do in Wisconsin? HENRY: Oh, Dad they worked themselves, and that was lumber country there. They went and worked in a sawmill. And then this lumber petered out and the sawmills moved away. Well then there was no work so they had to come out here. NBCO, #025, page 10 | HENRY cont.: Of course, Dad was sorry after pe come out here, there wasn t anything here either, except (beet?) work in summer, but he got a, I don t remember now if one of the companies went to California and one to Oregon. I don t know which one he worked for but anyhow, he could hardly goin' with them. He had a good job with that company, he was sorry he couldn t go with them, after he come out here and worked beets for a few days. MOLLY: So how did you start working beets? Did you see ads around town or did somebody... HENRY: Oh, these people here, their company would bring contracts in from Scottsbluff andpass them out. And this used to live here, he was one of them that got the contracts from the company then he distributed them to the people, whichever amount of acres you was able to work, he d give you a contract. MOLLY: Did your whole family work the beets? HENRY: Oh yeah. MOLLY: So about what year did you start doing that? HENRY: 1916. We come here in the Spring and then in May we went down to work. MOLLY: Did you like that sort of work? HENRY: Well, it was honest work, wasn t crazy about it, but that s all there was to do. Out there in hundred degree heat. Sixteen hours a day. We got up in the morning at four o clock and we went when the sun was down. MOLLY: What sort of work did you do actually? HENRY: Well, block and thinning 'em, that was the idea, spacin!' "em and then you had to thin them out and just leave one. That was usually the kids job, that was the hardest job. MOLLY: Did you do that standing up, or on your hands and knees, Ole 6 HENRY: Hands and knees, stoopin', whichever way, you got tired of stoopin' you d get on your hands and knees, get tired of that, sometimes it was too hot to be on your hands and knees, you d stoop, get up and stoop, the ground would be so hot vou couldn t crawl it. MOLLY: Did you ever feel that it was unfair that you had to work as a child? HENRY: No, cause we was used to workin! all our lives. worked all the time. It was nothin' new to me. MOLLY: What about the idea of working that didn t belong to you? NBCO, #025, page 11 MOLLY cont.: Was that hard to do? HENRY : No, no, that s no problem there. MOLLY: Were you paid as a family? HENRY: We got paid by the acre. It was piece work. MOLLY: And how many acres did you usually do? HENRY: Oh, we were first here and out there we had sixty acres, with six of us. Then during the war, 1918, there was four of us and we had 86 acres. We got smart. MOLLY: What time period of the year were you out in the beet fields? HENRY: Well, usually went out (end of tape) HENRY : 1918, during the war, we got $35 00 an acre, and boy everybody was makin' the money. That s what paid for all these homes and the same in South Bottom. That old man next door here, he come back with that family of his, he worked over a hundred acres, he banked $3 000 00 cash money! MOLLY: That was pretty good back then. HENRY: Yeah, had the kids go out and get jobs in these hotels and that and they earned their living during the winter. MOLLY: How did you get out to the beet fields? HENRY: Railroad. The company they d hire a train, a whole train, get on these coaches , it was as big as this Amtrak, if not bigger. They d have box cars in there, mixed in there, took all your baggage and furniture, what you d need out there and everything. Special train that hauled us out there and then they start at Bridgeport, distribute them, unload ‘em there and then out on in to Wyoming. MOLLY: About how long did it take to get out? Did you say Scottsbluff, is that where you went? HENRY: Oh, we d leave here in the afternoon, be there by next noon. MOLLY: What did you do on the train? HENRY: Oh, nothin’. Just sit there and - The young fellas they d usually have a car, an he young folks, well, they d dance, they d have dances there, all the way out. MOLLY: Really? On the train? HENRY: Yeah, dances and had crap games. MOLLY: That doesn t sound like nothin’. HENRY: But us kids, we d just sit there and take in the scenery. NBCO, #025, page 12 MOLLY: What sort of instruments did they have along with them? HENRY: Accordions, ces MOLLY: Did anybody have bellalikas, or dulcimers or anything like that? HENRY: Well, they didn t on the train. That old man used to live over there, Old Man (Lider? ) he played dulcimer at these weddings. MOLLY: Did anybody eat sunflower seeds on the train? HENRY: Oh, yes, plenty of 'em. It was like that one brakeman said, it was on the train, he said, one of the guys asked him, "How ya gonna clean these cars?" He said, "We ll take 'em to the roundhouse, we ve got a crane, turn 'em upside down so you can sleep in 'em." Get the sunflower seeds out. MOLLY: About how thick would you say they were on the floor? HENRY: Sometimes on some of them floors. MOLLY: What kind of accomodations did you have out in the beet fields? Where did you live? HENRY: We just had shacks. MOLLY: Were they pretty bad or were they livable? HENRY: They were livable, oh sometimes you hadda fix 'em up yourself. The farmer d give you materials and you d fix ‘em up yourself. We lived, uh, we worked a couple years there ae We lived in a log house and that was nice, that was warm in the fall in the cool weather, and cooler in summer. It was Mrs. Haig s log house, her and her husband and her dad come from England and homesteaded all that valley there, they had builded it. And all those years and we lived in it. It was really nice. She, uh, her husband was a brother to the great General Haig from England, you know, in the World War, they was brothers. I, uh, worked for royalty out there, worked for her quite a while. She had land in England yet, a hundred and eighty acres, she said. I think it was every two years, she had to go back there and register or she would lose that farm. And her kids, Phillis and Julia and Henry went to school over in England. Didn t let ‘em go to school here, had to go to school in England, dear ol' England. MOLLY: How many years did you work the beet fields? HENRY: About seven years. MOLLY: Then why did you stop? HENRY: Well, you get jobs in town and I went back to Wisconsin and I worked there, then I come back here and I started working for the University Power Plant there, there for 50 years. That s where I retired from. NBCO, #025, page 13 MOLLY: So where did your family live when they were in Lincoln? HENRY: Well, we lived here mostly. MOLLY: So this was your family home, too? HENRY: Yeah, we lived along here New Hampshire Street, used to call the yellow house We lived in that center house, the one ear Then, well then Dad bought this one, and before thatw @Itved one winter back on Eighth Street there, the bull eine(?). HENRY: Well, we lived in the front, see that was five rooms, yeah. We had the three front rooms, Jake Weisburger lived in the two back rooms. HENRY: It was a man by the name of Rogers, that s what they all said, they were Roger houses. MOLLY: You also mentioned that you lived in the bull dog ranch. HENRY: Yeah, there on 8th Street. MOLLY: What would you say would be the boundaries of the bull dog range, as far as streets went and the like, where did it run, from which street? HENRY: Well, the railroad track and everything on that side at that time was called bull ring. HENRY: Gosh, I don t know, probably couple a dozenat that time. HENRY: There weren t no businesses down there. MOLLY: Were the houses really in a circle? HENRY: No, no, it s streets. They was lined up in streets. MOLLY: Would you say there was any difference in the quality of houses that were there and the rest of the neighborhood? Or they were nice houses, too? HENRY: They were nice houses. MOLLY: Why did you: say that? HENRY ; I hope you ain t related to her. I talked to, was at a party one time this woman said, "Well, we re very good friends." I said, "I can t help that." MOLLY: Was she mean? HENRY: She was a mean old hag. NBCO, #025, page 15 MOLLY: Remember anything she did? HENRY: Oh, I didn t have any trouble with her, because I avoided her. HENRY: Well, she was short and chubby in build, she was grayhaired, I think, she wore a wig cause her hair was the same all the time, color and everything. MOLLY: Was she the type would call up the parents and complain apouyt the kids? HENRY: No, she d just take 'em off and give 'em a beatin'. She didn t complain. MOLLY: So people were afraid to run into her. Were all the teachers women, too? HENRY: Oh, yeah. Oh, we had a nice teacher, Mrs. Taylor. She was Irish. MOLLY: What sort of things did you learn in school? HENRY: Well, it was arithametic, reading, history, hygiene and everything else. HENRY: Well, they used to have German classes, up 'til the War then they had to quit ‘em. MOLLY: Did they quit 'em because of the War? MOLLY: Did you speak German at home? HENRY: Well, we had to, cause the fclks couldn t talk English. MOLLY: They never could? HENRY: No, they never learned it. MOLLY: Did you speak German among your friends when you were playing outside or anything like that? HENRY: Oh, a lot of times, yeah. NBCO, #025, page 17 MOLLY: What sort of games did you play? HENRY: Oh, same as kids now. Well, they don t play the games we used to, like kitzi and marbles and that, they don t play that anymore, the kids, that we used to play. MOLLY: What s tippy? HENRY: Well, it s a piece of broomstick about that long, they d sharpen it on each end and they rings there, knock it up and make your points. it was hard on windows. MOLLY: Did you ever break any windows? HENRY: I didn t, no. I know a lot of ‘em did when they played too close to the house or somethin'. MOLLY: Was that played any particular time of the year? HENRY: Yeah, Spring. MOLLY: Did you ever play ? HENRY: Yeah, that was a game, baseball. MOLLY: Did the girls play, too, or was it just the boys? HENRY: JuUst the boys. Bill Curtis had told me about that and he must have lived inthis neighborhood about the same time you did. HENRY: He lived right across the street, but I don t remember them having a race track, MOLLY: So, you did belong to Reverend Maul s church. How often did you have to go to church? HENRY: We had to go every, until we were confirmed, every Sunday. MOLLY: How was the seating arrangement in the chureh? HENRY: Oh, the same as any the other, the same thing. MOLLY: It wasn t divided between men on one side? HENRY: Oh, yeah, it was, yeah, until Maul was gone. Well, I think I started that, to mix up the people. Mr. Heckle, he worked at the Stadium a carpenter there, and we used to walk home evenings together. He was quite a guy. Talk about the church there. We was talking about it one night, he was one of the officers, and I said, "Jake, why in the hell why don t you make a motion to mix up the people." JI said in Wisconsin that church we belonged NBCO, #025, page 18 HENRY cont: to, the whole family sat together. And they took care of their own kids, discipline. I said, here, kids go upstairs, and the man that s got charge up there, they aggravate the life out of him, and the people can t hear the minister down below. Yeah, that s the way that Old Man Bush had that job one time, he said, "Never again." I said, this way each one takes care of his own kids. I said, you know who the kids are that s raisin' hell up there. He said, "Yeah, I m gonna bring it up, that s a good idea." Bigod, wasn t long after that, and they started mixin' up. MOLLY: Do you know why they ever separated them in the first place? HENRY: I don t know why, what the heck the idea was. MOLLY: They didn t do that in the old country? HENRY: Yes, that s probably why they done it here. Yeah, that was same thing out there. MOLLY: Do you recall any special times that they rang the church bells, aside from when church was about to start? HENRY: Well, the only time they, was Saturday evenings, at sundown they d ring, and Sunday evening. MOLLY: Did they ever ring when people died? HENRY: Yeah, and then they d ring 'em, I think, it was stopped that. They d ring 'em when the Lord s Prayer was said in church, and didn t know what the idea was! Well, we had a guy there at work once, he asked me about that. I said when you go to a doctor s office, or a lot of these businesses, they had a picture on the wall, it was a man and a woman standing in the field with their heads bowed, and he said, yeah, I ve seen that in doctor s office quite a lot. And I said, that s it. In the old country they did that, when the people that was out in the country had to work, when the Lord s Prayer was said in church, the bell would ring, then these people would stop work and say the Lord s Prayer along with 'em. HENRY: About sundown, six o clock they d usually ring ‘em. Well, that was in the old country, too, and then when they done ringin' that was the end of your work until they rung Sunday night. MOLLY: So, you were a member of the old St. John s that was at 10th and New Hampshire, and then were you part of the group that went over to the new St. John s? NBCO, #025, page 19 HENRY: Yeah. MOLLY: What denomination was that church? Was that Lutheran? HENRY: Yeah, it was supposed to be Lutheran. Well then it was mixed, it was Lutheran and Reform. MOLLY: Do you recall why some of the people left the first St. John s to start the second one? HENRY: I don t know why, I guess they just felt they didn t feel at home over there or somethin'. MOLLY: And then what happened to the old one, after some of the people left, did it go on, with the other members that had stayed? HENRY: No, when we joined that other one there, then some of them joined this other one over here, "s church. MOLLY: So then the church just stood empty? HENRY: Yeah, it s empty. MOLLY: Did you belong to the Brotherhood? HENRY: No. MOLLY: Do you know anything about it? Did you ever hear about it at all, I mean, know of people... ; HENRY: I didn t pay no attention to that. MOLLY: Now, you had mentioned a store over on 14th, did you ever hear of a Nagle(?) owning that store? Was that later than the man you were talking about or before? HENRY: Yeah, that s right, Masers over here, well that was a basket store at first. And they couldn t make a go of it, so Masers bought it. Yeah, I forgot about that, Masers. And down there. HENRY: Well, there used to be among the young folks, datin' the girls. MOLLY: So, who didn t want who to date? Whose girls? Ok Mitch, would you if you can, recall for us your earliest childhood. MITCH TAVLIN: I was born in Grodno Poland. As you know, Poland did not become a nation until the Treaty of Versailles in 1918. At the time we came over was a period known as the Great Migration from Eastern Europe to the United States. In fact from 1900 to 1920 approximately 14 500 000 peopie came from Eastern Europe to settle in the United States. My Father came to the United States in 1910. Two years later, my mother, together with my 3 brothers and one sister came to Lincoln, Nebraska. We left from the port of Bremen and landed at Galveston, Texas. We came to Lincoln in January of 1912. For a short period we lived on North i5* street, i don t recall the exact address, but it would be in about the 10 hundred block. We lived there several months and then moved to 1203 North 7‘ Street. At that time, the area was known as 7‘ and Z Street. It is now the corner of 7 Street and Charleston. I attended Hayward school, elementary school, until 1920 at which time | transferred to Lincoln High School. I attended Lincoin High School until June of 1923, graduated at that time. My first job was as a delivery truck driver for Grocery Store. I kept that job for 3 months and left it to go to work at a garage for the brothers at 1137, excuse me, 1237 P Street. I worked there exactly 18 months and left the day before Decoration Day, 1926 and went to work for Lou Polsky as a used car salesman. I worked for Lou Polsky for 6 years to the day and left the day before Decoration day, 1932 to open my own used car business. My brother joined me in the used car business the following year and we conducted our business as a partnership until December of 1939 at which time I purchased a liquor store. I conducted my liquor business for approximately 3 years and sold the store in October of 1942 at which time I entered the United States Army. I attended the Ordnance school, Proving grounds and was commissioned a 24 lieutenant in the Ordnance Corp on July 23, 1943. After attending supply school at Fort Lee, Virginia I was shipped overseas on the William H. Jackson, a liberty ship. We arrived at Oran in Algeria in November, 1943. I spent 2 weeks at Oran, the capitol of Algeria and then transferred to Camp Huxted which is located just outside Cairo. I was at Cairo for 2 weeks at which time I was transferred to Tehran, in Iran. | arrive in Tehran on Christmas Eve, 1943. I joined the 34315t Ordnance medium maintenance company at Iran 3 days later and served there until the day before Thanksgiving, 1944 at which time | was given a 30 day temporary duty to return to the United States. When I disembarked in Hoboken, NJ at Fort Dix in Hoboken, I received orders to report for overseas duty in a tempered climate outside the United States at the expiration of my 30 days temporary leave, my temporary duty. Two days before I was to report for my next trip overseas, I checked in at Winter General Hospital, Topeka, Kansas for major surgery. I was in Winter General Hospital for 3 weeks after which I rejoined the company to which I was originally assigned at Camp Shelby, Mississippi. My unit the 3431st Ordnance medium maintenance company was the first unit brought back to the United States under what was termed a redeployment program. This was in March of 1945. After 3 months duty at Camp Shelby I was transferred to 416th heavy ordnance maintenance company at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. I remained at North Carolina until the following March when | was separated from the service with a rank of Captain and | returned home. I then embarked on my first love, which was the used car business and 4 years later I bought a piece of ground at 40 & O Street and built a motel which I ve operated for 7 years. I sold my interest in the motel and have devoted the last 40 years to the wine and liquor business. I sold my liquor business on December 18, 1978 and since that time I have been semiretired. JO MILLER: Can you tell us any type of boyhood memories you remember living down here? MITCH: The memories of my childhood do not bring back pleasant events or occurrences. We were brought up under conditions of abject poverty. My dad insisted that he wanted to be his own boss and wanted to be a farmer. And since we observed the European custom of obeying the parents, we of course joined him in his efforts. He had difficulty ekeing out a living, trying to grow crops on scrubby ground and of course, we kept cows which | milked. And we sold the milk after my mother had bottled it and took it out, hitched up a horse and buggy and took it out to make home deliveries. I continued working at home until I was 16 years old after which time I left and tried to find work elsewhere. The conditions at home were not pleasant. People who complain while living at the poverty level today actually are living in luxury compared to the conditions under which we lived. We had as you know, no plumbing, no running water, no electricity, and of course no automobiles, no television, no radio and these are conditions to which I don t believe I care to return. These are conditions which do not develop character. On the contrary, they destroy initiative and are destructive in the developing the character of an individual. It s very tough to be poor. It doesn t make any difference, rich or poor, it s nice to have money. The house in which we lived at 1203 N 7 street was a house which my dad purchased from Louie Stine for $750. After the kids grew up. Of course, I forgot to mention that two of my brothers and sisters were born here, in fact were born in the house right across the street. My brother, John, was born in October of 1912 and my sister Ida was born in 1914. And of course, after the family was disbursed, my mother continued living in the house until about 1952 after which she moved to California to Long Beach, California where she made her home until she died on February 12, 1955. None of my brothers finished high school. I was the only one who graduated from High School. My second oldest brother left Lincoln in 1920 when he ran off to a circus, the Ringling Brothers Show. The following year, my mother had the Ringling show, their entire property attached. She filed a lawsuit against the Ringling Brothers circus for luring and enticing her son and debauching her son. The case involved considerable and lengthy litigation and was finally adjudicated by the payment of Ringling Brothers of $7 500 as damages to my mother for the loss of companionship of her son. My older brother was in the automobile business as was my younger brother. My youngest brother, John, was born in 1912 as] mentioned earlier. He entered the army in 1941. He was very seriously injured in the Battle of the Bulge on December 30, 1924 (date appears wrong) at which time he lost a leg and suffered other injuries. After 5 years of hospitalization, he returned to manage my liquor store for me. On November 21, 1961, a man entered my store just shortly before closing time, held up the store, shot my brother six times and killed him. My oldest brother, Lawrence, moved to California in 1946 and entered the outdoor advertising business. He died on February 14, 1949. He was at that time, 47 years of age. My next younger brother, Harry, also went to California after he was separated from the service. He too went into the outdoor advertising business. He died January 17, 1979, just two days after his 69‘ birthday. My second oldest brother the one who took off with the circus lives in New York City. He s now in the advertising business. My oider sister, Sadie, is retired and livesin Wayne, Nebraska. My younger sister, Idais employed at the Omaha Police Department Jo MILLER: Tell us about the games that you played when you were small. MITCH: The games we played would probably be recognized today because they are games which we ah arranged among ourselves, among the kids. They were impromptu, pick up games they would be called. We would choose up teams, choose up sides, to play baseball, one arm cat, run sheep run, a game which was a colloquial game for this particular area called ticky, which would be hard to describe or identify today. And we had no organized recreation. In later years, the public schools maintained a summer recreation program. But, I didn t participate in it, so I can t tell you what games were played. JO MILLER: Can you tell us special foods you had on holidays? MITCH: Holidays of course, being a member of a Jewish family, we served those that were traditional and indicative of the type of food served on those holidays. There was the Feast of Passover and many others. The life of a Jew is filled with holidays which occur periodically and at that time we did observe them. But I couidn t describe the food to you because you couldn t understand what it was. You don t know what a matzo ball is, what is, what chopped liver is. Unfortunately these are the types of food that I can t enjoy today because they aren t available. JO MILLER: Beings you lived here being a Jewish boy in the North bottoms and only Lutheran churches, did you go to church? MITCH: We went to services at a synagogue. The synagogue at that time was located at 18th & L Street. It was at that location until 1954 at which time the building was sold to the Lincoln Community Playhouse and a new edifice was construction at 3219 Sheridan. I belong to the conservative movement and T far Israel synagogue which is the name of my congregation is located now at 3254 and Sheridan. But the only time that we attended services was on the occasion of the high holidays. I had no religious training whatsoever and neither did any of the other members of my family, unfortunately. JO MILLER: Can you tell us about your children? How they have succeeded? MITCH: I have two boys. My older boy was born December 16, 1946. He sa graduate of Oklahoma City University. He s an AB and JD from the University of Nebraska. He has an LLN (or LLM) from Washington University in St. Louis. He was in private law practice for several years and now is a Senior Tax Supervisor for Touche Ross in the office located here in Lincoln, Nebraska. My younger son, John, has and AB and a JD from the University of Nebraska in which he graduated with high distinction. He s in private practice with the law firm of Heeley, Brown, Whelen & . Both of my sons are married. I have a grandson who will be 6 years old on the 12th of October . I m very lucky, very grateful and very thankful for all of my blessings.

NARRATOR: Yes, he came here on June 11, 1865. He and his sister and her husband, and two chidren, were with him. They landed at University Place, about 48th and Adams, the homestead goes from 48th Street down to 41st, and his laid to the north of Adams Street and my uncle s laid to the south. They homesteaded that. But they had to go to Nebraska City to get their homestead papers. They examined those things every five years. And they had been through, and they had two years until there was another examination. So he had to wait the seven years before he could get his final papers. And they had to go to Nebraska City - at the Court House. By the way, the courthouse stands in the square is the same courthouse he went to and got his papers. He was later married in that courthouse. INTERVIEWER: Now when did he . . . he was in the civil war, and got discharged. And then he came right to Nebraska from there? Their four children entered the University Place schools, where my mother graduated in 1895, being in the first class to graduate from Uni Place high school. My first memory of coming to Uni Place is when I was about 4 years old to visit my grandparents, who lived at the corner of 45th and Adams, 46th and Adams, or what used to be M Street. At that time Uni Place was quite a rural community. Many of the homes had barns in the back yards, and horses; however, there was a streetcar that came from Lincoln into University Place. My mother s brother worked for the Good¢ ice company and delivered ice when he was a young man on the streets of University Place by horse and wagon, always a trail of youngsters running behind him asking for slivers of ice. My grandparents moved here for the educational opportunities for their children since Wesleyan was a young college at that time and they had four growing children. Their home was conMildred Green Goth and Eleanor Green Weblemoe (064) 2 sidered the first modern home in University Place. The tub in the bathroom was a metal tub painted green with ball and claw legs. The toilet had a high tank with the pull chain. The lavatory hung on the wall with a wood framework around it and there was always Jack Rose soap in the soap bowl. (laughs) Grandmother moved over on 4503 Baldwin Street in 1919 after the school board purchased all the land in that block on N Street between ( ) the school and was between Adams and Cleveland, 46th to 47th, when they were still there. They were needing to enlarge the facilities since the first school had burned down and a large red brick building had been built, which was known as, is known now, as the Jackson building. The area where the grandparents lived is now the playground and at the time the house was built was to be used for the athletic field. One of my earliest I don t know what I can say one of my earliest memories was of walking towards 48th Street, which at that time was called Warren Avenue, and passing a small frame yellow home where a Negro family lived and there were always small children playing outside. That was my very first experience with seeing someone of a different color. But that house was moved then from 46th down to 44th, that little house, Grandma s house. Yes, Grandma s house. I d forgotten all about the Mr. and Mr. Henry daughter Bertha after graduating from University Place high school attended Wesleyan and then was employed in the millinery department by Miller and Paine for . Ed Green probably started working at Miller s shortly after 1900 where he was a floor walker and sold silks and satins on the first floor. I recently looked at the land deeds that are in the safety deposit box up at the bank, and they are very interesting long things = all hand written. So, that really is home for them, Our former science teacher over at Jackson High School, which is across the street, which is also a part of growing up in this house was fun because we were right across the street from the school, I saw Julius Young not very long ago and he said that he had found a photograph which had been taken with a box camera that his science class had made, A pinhole camera that was handcrafted in the class. They did a lot of things to the interior, too, to make it much more liveable and attractive. INTERVIEWER: (question inaudible) NARRATOR: Oh, that was about 1940, ‘41, INTERVIEWER: (inaudible) NARRATOR: I think, maybe, I was in my first year of college. I guess it s partly that Nebraska Wesleyan has been growing and has been a vital institution, that has meant that the neighborhood and the whole environs of University Place kept growing with the times, and had not been left to molder. It s been a very wonderful thing to come back to this house, to live in it, rather than being a real letdown, you know. . . Thomas Wolfe syndrome - you cannot go home again. In 1809 the population of Lincoln was about 25 000 and the Seventh Day Adventist church people out in this general area desired a college to educate their people. You see, at that time there weren t even very many high schools and then the Seventh Day Adventist people wanted their children to go to their own school, of course, to be in their own faith, just like the Methodists or the Presbyterians out at Hastings had their school and so on. Now that you may get the viewpoint, I may say that the organization of the Seventh Day Adventist church is by conferences, similar to the Methodists or the well, let s say similar to the Methodists; they. use that term conference and so they have the Nebraska conference and the Seventh Day Adventist people out in the Rocky Mountain area, the Colorado conference, and Kansas conference and so on. And, although the headquarters of the Adventist church at this time was Battle Creek, Michigan, and yet this was the largest area, largest concentration, of Seventh Day Adventists, was right here in the middle west. Roughly a third of the Adventists were right Everett Dick, Ph D. (083a and b) 2 here in this area that was later on to support Union College. And many, many people were moving west at that time, just the regular frontier development as it occurred in the United States at that time. And, whereas about the third of the Adventists in this area at that time, now it s only a small portion of them because the population sweep has gone on west; they re out in California now and many of them in Colorado and the North Pacific area and so on. But this was really quite a concentration of Adventists at that time, although there weren t too many of them, only about 27 000 all told in the world at that time. Now each of these conferences wanted a college. They thought that they d like to have a college. And now the second largest conference in the world at that time was the Kansas conference. Only Michigan was bigger. And Michigan, of course, had its Battle Creek College. And then Minnesota was almost as big as Kansas and they wanted a school. And Iowa the same. Now the man in charge of the educational program in the Adventist church at this time was a man by the name of W W. Prescott, after whom Prescott Street out here is named, and he told the people, said, "Well, now, you ought not to try to have a conference for each state. We don t have enough of a constituency to warrant that. What we ought to do is join together and perhaps have one northwest school and one southwest school." Northwest would be the Dakotas and Minnesota and Wisconsin. Southwest, of course, would be these Missouri, Kansas, Nebraska and Colorado. And, as they talked that over, they said, "Well, that s too many, even. Just one would be enough." And so in Kansas in the summer of 1889, they finally persuaded the Kansans that it would be alright to have one. And that was a pretty hard job because you know how it is, how provincial people are and they well, we just want one college and it s got to be here in Kansas"! (laughs and the Minnesota people felt the same way about Minnesota. But they finally decided that they would do that and they got Minnesota to agree and so the general conference, with its headquarters in Battle Creek at that time, decided that they would build a school for them, at a cost of $50 000, and they said, "The general conference will give $20 000 and these conferences out here should give $30 000."' And the conference involved then was the Dakota conference, as North and South Dakota were together at that time, the Dakota conference, Iowa, Nebraska, Missouri and Colorado, and they were to make up this $30 000. Everett Dick, Ph D. (083a and b) 3 A locating committee then was appointed. Now this was all the summer of 1889 that I m speaking of. A locating committee was appointed, with a few representatives from the general conference and the presidents of these conferences here, and they sent word out to the let it be known that the Adventists were going to build a college and "what will you offer to have the college located at your area?" Well, it was quite the thing in those days, you know, for the different cities to try to have a college. That would be a good thing. If there was a campus, they could have a college. And so they had several cities that wanted this college. Fremont wanted it; York, out here; Omaha; Atlantic, Iowa; Wichita, Kansas; did I say Omaha Omaha; and Des Moines was very anxious to have it. So the locating committee was ready to receive offers. Well, along toward the last, after these people had been visiting the different places to see whether they thought that these places would be a good place for the college, why, Lincoln sent a delegation, along toward the last, sent a delegation over to Des Moines where the brothers were meeting. And among this delegation was Professor Hitchcock of the University of Nebraska and a number of real estate men. The real estate people had formed what they called the Real Estate Exchange, the Lincoln Real Estate Exchange. Now these were real estate people that just wanted to make some money out of this thing, and not illegitimate necessarily, but I mean, they saw here s this chance to make good business deals, they could get this college out here. This area is known es Hazelhurst because Howard Smith started this addition and built their house but his wife decided on the Fox house on 38th. Howard Smith s wife s name was Hazel and therefore he named the addition after her. There is a Hazelhurst addition #1 and #2.
